Since the important links of this story are made up of dreams, it is appropriate to give a note here on the reality of dreams and of dreams that come from the self (ahlam).

A Muslim must necessarily hold the belief that some dreams contain explicit prediction about the near or distant future, because in this surah the dream of Yusuf, the dreams of Yusuf's two companions, and the dream of the king of Egypt, together with their mention, clearly necessitate that dreams can contain prediction. Furthermore, each of us sees such dreams and glad tidings in our personal lives, and they prove true, so true that a person cannot deny the reality of dreams, because in practice everyone finds this reality present. For belief in dreams, this surah and the explicit statements of the Quran are sufficient, but the other matter we have mentioned is also a practical and experiential reality, and it is not possible to deny it. The question then is: what is the reality of dreams? Psychological researchers have said that dreams are in fact reflections of a person's hidden and latent desires. This is indeed one aspect of dreams, but it is not the interpretation of all dreams. Freud, despite his complete irreligion and complete obstinacy, accepts that some dreams certainly hold the status of prediction.

The question is: what is the nature of these glad tidings? We accept that whether we can understand the reality of dreams or not, there is no doubt that some dreams are extremely true. Our aim is that man is a wondrous creation of Allah, and that we may come to know some aspects of the laws and wisdom that Allah has deposited within his existence.

We explain the reality of such true dreams in this way: we cannot perceive the events and occurrences of the past and future because a veil of time and space stands between us and them, or because a thing is present yet hidden from our sight. The factor of time removes the past and future from our view, just as the factor of place keeps a distant presence beyond our knowledge. Sometimes senses within a person awaken or become strengthened, which can see ahead by tearing through the veils of time, but their form is vague. This is not complete knowledge, but it is a glimpse (istishaf). For some people this is attained even while awake, and for some people this perception occurs in sleep. Yet we know neither the reality of this nor the reality of time. Likewise, space, which is composed of matter, is also not well known to us.

"Wa ma utitum min al-ʿilmi illa qalila" ("And you have been given only a little knowledge"). In any case, Yusuf saw the dream and its interpretation is coming.

As for me, I would say that I can deny everything, but I cannot deny an event that happened to me personally. I saw in a dream that one of my niece's eyes had blood in them and she could not see. I wrote a letter home asking about her eyes, what had happened to her. They wrote back that she had a condition that was not visible from outside. Apparently her eyes looked fine, but she could not see anything at all, and that she was being treated. My dream was true, and there is much more besides, which need not be mentioned.

Now the curtain falls, and Prophet Ya'qub and Prophet Yusuf recede into the background. Another scene comes into view, in which the brothers of Yusuf appear in motion. Their movements show that important events are about to take place.

These opening words are sufficient to draw the reader's attention, alert them, and stir them to the importance of the matter. These words are like the moment when the curtain is raised on a stage and what is upon the stage becomes visible before the eyes, because immediately after these words the brothers of Yusuf are seen speaking, and in this dialogue they are seen plotting against Yusuf.

Here the question arises whether it is known from this passage that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) had related his dream to his brothers, as the Old Testament says, or not. From the context of the speech, no such thing is apparent here, because their accusation is that Prophet Ya'qub loves Yusuf and his full brother more than them. Had they known that Prophet Yusuf had seen a dream, its mention would certainly have come from their tongues. And thus they would also have been excused for their malice and envy. For Prophet Ya'qub's advice to Yusuf to keep the dream hidden was given precisely because, in view of other circumstances, he knew that they would be inflamed with jealousy, and this envy and malice were bound to occur, since it was only by passing through that furnace that Prophet Yusuf was to reach his appointed station. The circumstances of his life, the circumstances of his family, and the fact that he was born to Prophet Ya'qub in his old age and was the youngest, not to mention that in old age a man has great affection for small children, especially when those small children are the offspring of a stepmother and a younger mother.

That is, your taking him away grieves me, and I cannot bear separation from him. Now they adopted a highly effective style again to refute this apprehension: how is it possible that, with such a large group present, a wolf should devour Yusuf? How could this be possible? Otherwise we would indeed be utterly useless and in loss.

As a result of this dialogue, despite all his apprehensions, Hadrat Yaqub was compelled to let Yusuf go with them, and thus the further links of the story came to pass in accordance with the decree of Allah.

Now these men are taking him along, and they are carrying out that wicked plot. And Allah is placing in the heart of this child the thought that this is a trial, that it will come to an end, and that, God willing, he will survive and will himself inform his heedless brothers about it.

It was settled among them that Yusuf should now be thrown into the well, where he would be kept out of their sight. Anyone can imagine what Yusuf must have gone through at that time, as all these brothers together were casting this weak child into the well. He would have seen his own death approaching, and the brothers' looks would have changed. In that state of helplessness and forlornness, only Allah's help comes, and Allah places in their hearts tranquility and composure: that you will survive, you will tell them what you had done, and that, in such circumstances, this child who is being thrown into the well will one day become the ruler of the kingdom.

Now let us leave Yusuf in that dark well for a moment and go to Kan'an. He is now under Allah's protection and care until Allah brings him out from there. Now the curtain falls, and these people, after committing such an evil deed, stand before their father. Let us observe their pretence:

In the evening they came weeping to their father and said, "Father, we went off racing one another, and we had left Yusuf by our belongings, and then a wolf came and devoured him. Hearing this, their father said, "Rather, your own selves have made a great matter easy for you. So patience is most fitting, and it is Allah whose help is sought against what you describe."

In their hearts a fire of spite was burning, and these people were fabricating lie upon lie. Had they had any control over their nerves, they would never have done such a thing; they would not have begun this vile plot at all. And when Ya'qub (ʿalayhi al-salam) had trusted them and entrusted Yusuf to their care, they should have desisted. But Yusuf had now become intolerable to them, and they were thinking that this was the best opportunity for them to carry out their black deed. Moreover, they had obtained the excuse of the wolf from Ya'qub's own words, and the clearest proof of their hastiness and immaturity is that they devised no other excuse beyond their father's fear, even though it was only the day before that Ya'qub had frightened them with that very pretext and they had replied that they were a strong band. Now they are offering that same excuse. Apparently this excuse is not reasonable: that the very thing they were warned about at night should be presented as an excuse in the morning. Then, what further proof of their shallowness could there be than that they brought a shirt smeared with blood? And it is evident that at first glance this was a very flimsy pretext, yet they presented this lie:

This dark well was beside a public road. People around the public road always go out in times of need in search of water, and rainwater also collects in such wells. Sometimes the well is dry as well.

"وجاءت سيارة" – "And a caravan came along." In Arabic, a caravan is called sayyarah because sayr means to travel, and a caravan is also on a long journey. It is also called nashanah, hawalah and fannamah.

Here, within the flow of the narrative, the detail that Yusuf clung to the bucket is omitted, because it is entirely evident, and the aim here is to confront the reader with a surprising situation. Lesson No. 107: At a Glance

This lesson comprises the second phase of the story. Yusuf (peace be upon him) has now reached Egypt. He has been sold as a slave, but the man who purchased him saw that this boy was exceptionally promising. (A promising sapling shows its beauty in its tender leaves.) He then gave instructions to his wife regarding him, that this boy is extraordinary. From here the interpretation of Yusuf's dream begins.

However, before reaching maturity, Yusuf faced another kind of trial. Allah had granted Yusuf knowledge and wisdom befitting the office of prophethood, and this trial was such that only the grace and mercy of Allah could save anyone in it. Yusuf was being raised in the free environment of the upper classes. Such classes are generally given to luxury and immorality, and many of their young men fall into waywardness. By the sheer grace of Allah, Yusuf emerged from that corrupt environment with his chastity intact. For him, this hardship was no less than the earlier trials.

Lesson No. 107: Explanation of the Verses

Verses 21 to 34

Commentary on verse 21: We have not yet been told who bought him. However, it will be mentioned a little later that the buyer was the Aziz of Egypt. It is said that he was among the notables of Egypt. But we come to know that Yusuf was given the opportunity to establish himself. Now the days of distress and hardship have passed, and better days than ever are coming for him.

"Akrimi mathwahu" means "Honour his residence" (mathwa is a noun of place from thawa, meaning the place where one spends the night and stays). Honouring the residence refers to honouring him himself. But the phrase "honour his place of stay" is more emphatic than saying "honour him": it means not only honouring his person but also honouring his place of residence. Earlier, his place of residence was a blind well, surrounded by dangers from every side, with calamities upon calamities; and now he has a secure place here.

The Aziz of Egypt tells his wife what hopes he attaches to this boy.

"Asa an yanfa'anaa aw nattakhidhahu waladan": Perhaps he will be useful to us, or we may adopt him as a son. As some narrations state, perhaps he had no son. This is why he expressed the intention that if this boy proved to be discerning, they would adopt him as a son, as was evident from Yusuf's temperament and manners; later he proved to be a man of sound judgment.

Here the narrative of events is paused, and a brief commentary comes in between, explaining that these arrangements were made by Allah so that Yusuf's position in Egypt would be firmly established. Now Yusuf has secured a place in the heart of this buyer and in his household, the period of his advancement has begun, and later he will be placed in this high society and given opportunities to demonstrate his sound judgment. At the same time, it is made clear that Allah has complete control over all His affairs, and that Allah's plans are carried out exactly as He wills.

"Wa kadhalika makkannaa li-Yusufa fil-ardi wa linu'allimahu min ta'wili al-ahadith; wallahu ghalibun 'ala amrihi wa lakinna akthara an-nasi la ya'lamoon": In this way We established Yusuf in that land and made arrangements for teaching him the interpretation of events. Allah accomplishes His affair, but most people do not know.

How so? See what plot Yusuf's brothers devised against him, what Allah planned for him, and what came to pass. Allah's will prevailed, because Allah has control over all affairs; therefore their schemes were brought to nothing, and Allah's plan for Yusuf succeeded.

Yet most people do not recognise this truth: that what Allah wills comes to pass, and that nothing happens by the wishes of people.

Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 22:

Allah gave Yusuf (peace be upon him) the ability to make correct decisions in every matter, and he would know the outcomes of events in advance. He knew the interpretation of dreams very well. The meaning of ta'wil (interpretation, explanation of the ultimate meaning or outcome) of ahadith and ta'wil of ru'ya (dreams) may also be general, meaning that he would resolve all the affairs of life very well. This discernment was given to him because of his goodness and his good conduct, and Allah thus rewards the muhsinin (those who do good).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 12, verse 23:

Now Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) faces the most severe test of his life, the hardest trial he has ever known. This trial comes at a time when Allah has already granted him knowledge and the ability to make sound judgments, so that through these he may overcome his difficulties and emerge triumphant. For he is a righteous and pure young man, and this is Allah's way of dealing with those who do good.

Now observe this dangerous scene:

"At last Yusuf and she raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind. At the door they found her husband. Seeing him, the woman said: 'What is the punishment for one who intends evil against your wife, other than imprisonment or a painful punishment?' Yusuf said: 'It was she who sought to seduce me.' A witness from her own family testified: 'If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is a liar; but if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is truthful.' When the husband saw that Yusuf's shirt was torn from the back, he said: 'This is one of your women's schemes; indeed, the guile of you women is mighty. Yusuf, overlook this matter. And you, woman, ask forgiveness for your sin, for you were surely among the wrongdoers.'"

...

Here the Qur'an does not tell us her age, nor the age of Yusuf. We can only estimate both ages from conjecture.

When the caravan took up Yusuf, he was a boy. He was sold in Egypt, so his age was about fourteen years, because in Arabic the word ghulam is used for boys of about that age. Thereafter, for people of that age the words fata and shab are used, and after that the word rajul is used. Only at such an age could Yaqub say that a wolf might devour him. At that time the wife of the Aziz of Egypt was a single wife, and it also appears that she had no children.

The phrase "au nattakhidhahu waladan" also shows that most likely they had no children. The idea of adopting a son arises only when one has no offspring, or when a person has despaired that children can still be born and then thinks of adoption. So it appears that a considerable time had passed since this couple's marriage, and that they had probably despaired of children. In any case, it is not possible that the prime minister of Egypt was under forty years of age, and at that time his wife could in no way have been under thirty.

In any event, the most probable conjecture is that Yusuf was fifteen years old and the wife of the Aziz was forty years old. The circumstances roughly indicate that the ages of the two parties to this event were these. Another indication that the woman was mature is that the stance she took regarding this event is the stance of a mature and bold woman, one who keeps complete control over the threads of her scheme. The comments of Egyptian women also show that she was an older woman.

"Imra'at al-Aziz turawidu fatāhā" means: the wife of the Aziz is pursuing her young servant. Although fata is used for a servant, it is also used for a slave because it carries the sense of youthful excellence (futuwwah), and Yusuf was such a person. In any case, the testimony of the circumstances and conditions supports these facts.

We are conducting this discussion so that a definite conclusion may be drawn from it: that this woman did not merely try to seduce Yusuf in a single incident, as the Qur'an mentions, but that Prophet Yusuf remained under this trial continuously from his years of adolescence, because he was in the house of the prime minister, and at that time the woman was between thirty and forty years of age. The conditions of that society are well understood from the words of her husband: "Yusuf, overlook this matter. And you, woman, ask forgiveness for your sin, for you were surely among the wrongdoers."

Also, the gossip of women, that the wife of the Aziz was doing such-and-such, her counter-scheme, the arrangement of her banquet, Yusuf's appearance before them, their astonishment, and her remark: "Indeed I sought to seduce him, but he refrained. And if he does not do what I command him, he shall surely be imprisoned and become of the humbled ones." All this indicates the same.

Such a society, in which such matters are freely discussed, is a society of the upper class. Yusuf was caught in it as a slave and was being raised within it. And the age he was at is what is called a time of temptation and trial. This was Yusuf's long and arduous test, and in it he remained steadfast. He emerged from it triumphant and succeeded against the temptations of that society and that age. If one considers his age and the woman's age, and that they were living in the same house, it becomes clear how long Yusuf endured these circumstances. Had this been only a single incident, he could have easily confronted it and it would not have been difficult for him, especially since the one sought is not the seeker; especially when a woman desires, a man cannot refuse, and in this incident the woman was the one desiring.

After this preface, now the explanation of the verses.

"And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors and said: 'Come, here I am for you.'"

This time the woman openly tries to seduce Yusuf, and in it she clearly invites him to the final stage. Closing the doors happens at the final stage, and this woman has now reached that extreme; this is the final stage of physical desire.

"And she said: 'Come, here I am for you.'" This final, clear and open invitation is not the first time a woman has made such an invitation. It comes after great preliminaries. If a woman is not overcome by physical desire, she would never make such an invitation. Since the young man had lived in their house, his physical strength had gradually matured, and the woman's desires must have passed through many stages before she said "Come, here I am for you," and before this final stage Yusuf must have confronted some of her allurements.

He said: "I seek refuge in Allah! Indeed, my Lord has made my abode good. Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper." Yusuf said: "God forbid! Surely my Lord has given me a good station, and I shall not do this. Such wrongdoers never prosper." "God forbid, I seek Allah's protection; how could I do this?"

"Indeed, my Lord has made my abode good." My Lord has given me a good station. He rescued me from the dark well and placed me in an honourable position, in a household of such high standing.

"Indeed, the wrongdoers never prosper." Those who transgress the limits of Allah do not prosper, and what you are inviting me to is nothing but a transgression of the limits of Allah.

Here the Qur'an clarifies this matter, and clarifies it definitively: that Yusuf rejected, without hesitation, both the woman's enticing act and her open invitation to sin, shutting the doors. He remembered the limits set by Allah (hudud Allah) and remembered Allah's favours. Although the Qur'an expressed this invitation to sin not in vulgar words but in refined language, namely: وَلَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهٖ ۚ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوْلَآ اَنْ رَّاٰ بُرْهَانَ رَبِّهٖ : "She certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord."

This was the final stage, and all the commentators have written at length on it. Among the early commentators, some followed Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) and related numerous reports on this subject. These reports mention that Yusuf (peace be upon him), like an ordinary young man, was inclined toward that final act, was advancing, and Allah was showing him proof upon proof, yet he was not stopping. In that secluded chamber, the image of Ya'qub (Jacob) appeared, and he had bitten his finger between his teeth. And suddenly a tablet appeared before him on which Qur'anic verses were inscribed: verses saying, "Refrain from such an act." Yet he still did not stop, so Allah sent Jibril (Gabriel) (peace be upon him) and said, "Go and tell My servant that he is about to fall." He came and struck Yusuf on the chest with a blow. These and other such reports, which clearly show that they are fabricated and contrived.

As for the majority of commentators, they have said that the woman had resolved upon the sin, and Yusuf too would have resolved upon it had Allah's proof not become manifest to him, and then he gave up his resolve.

Sayyid Rashid Rida, in his tafsir al-Manar, refuted this interpretation of the majority of scholars. The real meaning, he holds, is that she was an oppressive mistress; she invited him to sin and beat him, because he had refused and thereby insulted her, and Yusuf responded to her aggression. Then he found it safer to flee, and she seized him and tore his shirt. The explanation that (hamm) means beating and that responding to a beating is a interpretation for which there is no evidence. It has been established as pure and clean only through effort. Yet this interpretation is not free of artificiality, and the Arabic words do not bear it.

After reflecting on these texts, what has occurred to me is this: Yusuf was living in one house with this experienced woman, and this continued over a long period, both before he was granted knowledge and wisdom and after.

What I understand from this verse is that it describes the final stage. That woman made efforts for a long time to entice him, and he refused. During this period Yusuf confronted these difficult circumstances, and the Qur'an in this verse mentions the final stages: that he adopted purity and saw the proof of his Lord. This struggle the Qur'an has described here very briefly and given it a brief place. It used appropriate and necessary words for it. It recorded the beginning and end of the struggle in such words that at the beginning he refused, and at the end he saw the proofs of Allah. But between the initial and final stages, it is possible that moments of weakness also came, and thus both realistic truth and a pure atmosphere were completed.

When studying these circumstances and texts, this idea came to my mind. It is close to human nature and temperament, and it is also in harmony with the office of prophethood. Yusuf was nonetheless a human being, and a chosen human being. For this reason his psychological inclination also ended, and he returned to a state of protection and complete refusal.

Allamah Zamakhshari says in al-Kashshaf: "The question is how a prophet could have hamm (intention) toward evil, and how he could resolve to do such an act. The answer is that it was a psychological inclination; the pressure of youthful desires is upon every human being. Here it is expressed as hamm and qasd (resolve) because in such circumstances a person faces intense pressure and the danger of resolve and resistance breaking, but Yusuf, after observing Allah's proofs, confronts this pressure. If this inclination had not existed and there had been no physical pressure, how would Yusuf have become praiseworthy by refraining from this act? For patience, endurance and reward for trial exist only when the person has strength and inclination within him."

Thus it was, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality; indeed he was of Our chosen servants: ﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنَصْرِفَ عَنْهُ السُّوءَ وَالْفَحْشَاءَ إِنَّهُ مِنْ عِبَادِنَا الْمُخْلَصِينَ﴾

And they both raced to the door: "At last Joseph and she ran toward the door, one behind the other." Joseph considered it wise to flee in order to free himself from her grip, and this woman too ran after him so that she might catch him, because she was still in a state of sexual frenzy.

﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾: "And she tore Joseph's shirt from behind." The shirt tore because of her pulling it, since her aim was to take him back from the door.

﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾: "At the door, the two of them found her husband present."

Here the woman now appears in the form of complete composure. The situation is such that suspicion may fall on either party, and the woman's answer is ready: she immediately puts the blame on the young man. ﴿She said: What is the punishment for one who intends evil to your wife?﴾: The woman said: "What is the punishment for the one who intends evil toward your household?" But since she had both affection for Joseph and fear that he might be killed, she herself proposes a mild punishment: ﴿Except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment﴾: "What other punishment could there be than that he be imprisoned or that he be given a painful torment?"

And Joseph (peace be upon him) immediately refutes the accusation, stating that it was she herself who tried to seduce him.

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 26–27:

Here the Qur'an clearly states that at this occasion a person from the woman's relatives was present, who gave a decision on the basis of circumstantial evidence (shahadat-e-ahwal, i.e. the existing indications), and the dispute ended.

﴿And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is one of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is one of the truthful."﴾

A person from her own family presented testimony (of indication): "If Yusuf's shirt is torn from the front, then the woman is truthful and he is a liar. And if his shirt is torn from the back, then the woman is a liar and he is truthful."

The question is: where did this witness give his testimony? Was he present with the husband at that time, or was an elderly person from the wife's family called after seeing the incident, and did the Aziz of Egypt place this matter before him, as often happens in such situations? This is especially so among high-ranking classes, whose blood is cool and whose moral values are loose.

Both of these may be possible, and the meaning is not affected. The judgment of this person is called testimony here because the positions of both parties were presented before him; he gave a legal opinion or a view, and it is called testimony because through testimony too a person reaches the truth. The testimony of the circumstances is this: if the shirt is torn from the front, it means the man was the aggressor and the woman was defending herself; therefore she is truthful and he is a liar. If the shirt is torn from the back, he was fleeing and she was pulling him back by it; therefore she is a liar and he is truthful. This person first presented the case of the woman's truthfulness, because she is the mistress and he is the slave; therefore it was appropriate that the matter favoring the master and the upper hand be mentioned first. In both cases, the circumstantial evidence exists.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 28:

When the husband saw that Yusuf's shirt was torn from behind, he would have understood that, according to the evidence of the circumstances, the woman was lying. It was she who had tried to seduce him, and it was she who had plotted to accuse him.

Here a glimpse of a "developed society" appears, and that a society centuries and thousands of years old. It seems as though it were the developed society of today. The first characteristic of this kind of society is that sexual scandals are overlooked in it; they are concealed. These are the important matters of such societies.

He said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Surely your guile is mighty." (Surah Yusuf 12:28) Yusuf, turn away from this matter. And you, woman, seek forgiveness for your sin; surely it was you who were at fault.

"Quite right, indeed the guile of women is mighty. Yusuf, overlook this; this is mere flattery. Seeing such an incident that stirs the blood, to say only that your guile is great, and that too in words where the guile of all women is described as fearsome, is in fact a praise of this woman: that she is a great schemer and a skilled operator, and that she has made a successful move."

Also addressed to Joseph, the same was said: "Ignore this" (a'rid 'an hadha). That is, "Overlook it. Leave this matter here, do not mention it, and keep the situation as it is. In a society of this kind, this is an important matter."

As for the woman, who had been caught red-handed, the comment directed to her was that you are a sinner, so seek forgiveness for your sins. These are the leading bureaucrats of that time and the hangers-on of the great. In every jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), such people are like this.

Now the curtain falls and this scene ends. In the context of the discourse, this stage has been presented with all its circumstances, impressions and allusions, but this delicate stage has been kept free from animal lust, and a most humane and dignified manner has been adopted.

The situation is that the separation between this woman and her slave-boy has not yet occurred. Events continue in their usual course, and in great palaces such events keep unfolding in just this way. But palaces have walls, and walls have ears. Feet and eyes are inside them; whatever happens within must surely come out, especially in the palaces of the high and privileged classes. Whatever takes place inside these palaces is talked about in people's gatherings and on everyone's tongue. For the people, it is the spicy masala of their nights.

The women of the city began to gossip among themselves that the wife of the Aziz was pursuing her young slave, that love had made her uncontrollable, and that in their view she was clearly making a mistake.

This talk and this gossip are exactly like what is the subject of conversation in every Jahili age. It is here, for the first time, that we learn that this woman is the wife of the Aziz of Egypt, and that the man who bought Yusuf in Egypt was the Aziz of Egypt, that is, the prime minister of Egypt. The name of that man and the name of his wife had been kept vague until now; now the name is mentioned because the whole of Egypt has become aware of this incident. ﴿And the women in the city said, "The wife of the Aziz is seeking to seduce her young slave from himself. He has captivated her heart with love. Indeed, we see her in manifest error."﴾ That is: the women of the city began to gossip among themselves that the wife of the Aziz was pursuing her young slave, that love had made her uncontrollable, and that in their view she was clearly making a mistake.

That is, the woman's state is that she is pursuing him. She has become a lovesick captive. The love of the slave has descended into the veil of her heart. Shaghaf (شغف) is the name for the membrane in which the heart is wrapped. But this conduct is not fitting for this woman: that being the first lady and the wife of the prime minister, she should fall in love with a Hebrew slave who is a purchased bondsman (the words "fatāhā" [her slave-boy] are mentioned so that, perhaps, free sexual relations were not so reproachable in that Jahili society, but relations with a Hebrew purchased slave were considered even more shameful).

Now that event occurs which can only take place among such so-called high classes. This willful woman presents another scene. She knows how she will respond to the cunning and propaganda of the women of Egypt. Let us now look at the following verses.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 31:

He invited those women to a banquet in his palace. The nature of this banquet shows that it was a gathering of highly cultured people. Such women are invited to banquets in palaces, and very elaborate foods are served. It also appears that, in accordance with the Eastern customs of that time, people ate while reclining on cushions. Accordingly, she arranged a place for eating where these women sat leaning on cushions. Then a knife was given to each one so that she might eat with it. This shows that in that age Egypt had advanced far ahead in terms of civilization and culture, and that people in the palaces lived a life of luxury. For the mention of the use of the knife thousands of years ago shows that Egyptian society had already advanced far ahead in material and cultural terms. While these women were busy cutting meat and fruit, Aziz's wife (ʿAzīza) ordered Yusuf to come forward: "Come out before them."

﴿She said, "Go out before them."﴾ She signalled to Yusuf to come out before those women.

﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed at him﴾ When those women cast their eyes upon him, they were astonished. On seeing him they were stunned, and awe overtook them.

﴿And cut their hands﴾ Out of sudden awe they wounded their own hands.

﴿And said, "Hāshā lillāh!"﴾ Spontaneously they exclaimed, "Ḥāshā lillāh!" Out of amazement at the creation of God's power, "Ḥāshā lillāh" is said. In fact, the expression Ḥāshā lillāh, a word of declaring God free from imperfection, is used on an occasion where a person is absolutely cleared of an accusation.

﴿This is not a human being; this is none but a noble angel.﴾ "This person is not a human; he is some noble angel." As we said in the introduction to this surah, these expressions show that some concepts of the religion of Islam had already spread in Egyptian society.

Now Aziz's wife became certain that she had won the field and had taken revenge on the women who had been speaking against her, and that these women themselves had been left terrified, astonished, and even stunned. Now she openly reveals herself before the women, describes her sexual scandal in detail before them, and feels no shame. Now she declares in a threatening tone that this person must act according to her will, otherwise... Now the manner of her speech is different.

"She said, 'That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused. And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be of the debased.'"

Here the wife of the Aziz says: "Behold, this is the one about whom you used to reproach me." Look at it! This is the very man regarding whom you were making remarks against me. See for yourselves. And take a look at your own condition as well: tell me, why have you become bewildered, distracted and beside yourselves?

"Indeed, I sought to entice him, but he kept himself chaste." She has been driven to this state by him: I tried very hard to lure him, yet he escapes. In the face of all my efforts and my schemes of temptation, he remains steadfast upon his principles. But, strangely, this woman of the high class of Egyptian society is openly expressing her sexual designs before all the women and even threatening him. "And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be of the debased."

Now this woman, besides the weapons of seduction that belong to the weaker sex, is proudly employing the means of coercion and threat as well. This threat is being openly given to Joseph in the gathering of women, and in front of those very women, each of whom is herself present with her own allurements. And this threat is being issued to him by his own mistress, so in such delicate and dangerous circumstances, help can be sought from the Lord, the Exalted, alone.

Sayyid Yusuf now does not only raise his hands in supplication against the wife of the Aziz, but the women of the high class of Egypt have now also fallen behind him. Because of their gestures and their words, all the women are falling over him. Now he turns to Allah in supplication, and against these trials he seeks Allah's help, and he fears that he is being lured from every side, and that at any moment weakness may appear in him. Therefore, in these circumstances and in such a severe trial, he is fearing.

﴿And if You do not turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and become one of the ignorant.﴾

"This is the call of a person who is aware of his own law, who knows that a human is a human. Although he is firm, his own weaknesses are also in his sight. Therefore he seeks further protection from Allah so that he may be able to face these trials with composure."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 34:

How Allah turned away their plots, so that they despaired of him. They devised many stratagems and carried out experiments, but he did not fall into their snare, for "the nest is high beyond the reach of the phoenix" (ʿUnqa rā buland ast āshiyāna). Another possibility is that these stirrings of sedition had no effect on the Prophet at all. Allah is Samiʿ and ʿAlim; He sees everything and hears everything. Here Hazrat Yusuf succeeded in this second trial and test of his life. (By the grace and mercy of Allah.)

This passage is the third link in the story, and it is the final stage of Prophet Yusuf's (peace be upon him) trials. After this link, the difficult days of Yusuf's life are coming to an end. Now there will be only ease and tranquility. His test will now take a different form. Previously he was tested through hardships; now he will be tested through a life of comfort and authority. In this link, his trial is taking place through imprisonment. It is a strange trial: he has been cleared of the accusation, yet he remains in prison. A guilty person can bear patience because he knows he has done wrong, but when an innocent person is imprisoned, the punishment is unbearable for him, even though in his heart he finds comfort in knowing he is innocent.

During this period, Allah's favours upon Yusuf have begun to appear. He has now been granted knowledge of the interpretation of dreams, a knowledge bestowed directly by Allah (ʿilm ladunni), and he has become skilled in the interpretation of events (taʾwil al-ahadith). At the very beginning of matters, he comes to know what their outcomes will be. Then, the arrangement for establishing Yusuf's innocence before the king is also being made: the king himself summons the women and conducts an inquiry. Now Yusuf's hidden capabilities are coming to light. He becomes the king's closest confidant, the holder of all authority, and the supreme ruler. And he reaches the station to which Allah had intended to raise him.

Lesson No. 108: Commentary on verses 35 to 52

In the atmosphere of palaces, under the shade of tyranny, in the courts of nobles, and within the systems of jahiliyyah, such decisions are made. They had seen with their own eyes the purity of Yusuf (peace be upon him). They had seen that this woman presented that angel-natured person before the gatherings of women and openly issued threats. All the women of Egypt were convinced that this woman was blinded by love for her servant and was roaming about proclaiming her infatuation. The pressure of these women upon Yusuf (peace be upon him) grew so great that he sought refuge in Allah. On the other hand, this woman was also determined about this matter and was declaring that Yusuf must fulfil her desire or else he would be humiliated in prisons; now he would either obey the command or go to jail.

After these circumstances, these people reached the conclusion that Yusuf should be imprisoned for a period of time. It is clearly apparent that this woman had now become despairing, while gossip had spread widely and the reputation of these so-called high households could be protected only by imprisoning the innocent one. For them this task was very easy. Since he had not fulfilled the desires of that refined woman, he was necessarily to go to prison, because that unfortunate woman had become defamed, and from every side there was gossip, and in every gathering she was the subject of talk.

Coming up in the context, it will become clear that these men were among the king's attendants and servants. The Qur'an does not give a detailed account of Prophet Yusuf's years in prison, but it is evident that his purity of character, goodness, seriousness and dignity became so widely known in the prison that he became an example among all the prisoners. He became the chief trustee for all the prisoners. Among these prisoners were also those who had been put in prison because of the royal displeasure, for they must have committed some fault in the royal palace and court. Accordingly, displeasure had temporarily fallen upon them. In any case, to move the story along quickly, the Qur'an omits the remaining details and mentions only two young men. These two young men came to Prophet Yusuf, presented their dreams before him, and made the request that he tell them the interpretation. Why did these people choose Prophet Yusuf for the interpretation of dreams? Because they saw that he was truthful, righteous, a worshipper, and a man of remembrance and reflection.

Two other slaves entered the prison along with him. One day one of them said, "I saw in a dream that I was pressing wine," and the other said, "I saw that bread was placed on my head and birds were eating from it." Both said, "Tell us its interpretation; we see that you are a righteous man." Now Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) found the opportunity to present his outlook on life before the prisoners. He would give them correct belief, for it is not forbidden for a prisoner to have sound belief. The ideological and practical training of prisoners is also necessary. Therefore Prophet Yusuf instructs them that the root of all evils is a corrupt system of life in which command and sovereignty belong to anyone other than Allah. Accordingly, he instructs them that to acknowledge other people as the lord of this earth, leaving Allah aside, is the true misguidance, and in this way rulers become Pharaohs.

Prophet Yusuf begins his speech with the subject in which his two companions in prison are interested. But he promises them that the discussion of their topic of interest will come a little later. He will tell them the correct interpretation of the dreams, because Allah has given him knowledge of this field, and He has given it because I worship Allah and neither I nor my forefathers associate anything with Allah. Thus Prophet Yusuf assures these people that he will tell them the interpretation of the dream, and that the religion of Prophet Yusuf is also a most upright religion.

The commentary shows how pleasing Prophet Yusuf's speech is, how he draws one point out of another, and how gently and delicately he speaks. In this whole story, this is the distinguishing feature of Prophet Yusuf's conversation.

﴿He said: No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is part of what my Lord has taught me.﴾ Yusuf said: Before the food that you are given here arrives, I will tell you the interpretation of your dreams. This is among the knowledge that my Lord has bestowed upon me.

This emphasis shows that Prophet Yusuf had been given a special knowledge in this matter, so that before the food arrives he would, by means of this particular knowledge, tell them the interpretation of their dreams. And this knowledge was given to him because in that age the science of dream interpretation had made considerable progress. "This is among the knowledge that my Lord has bestowed upon me": the Prophet used these words so that they would have a psychological effect on these people, and his words would sink into their hearts, and that, through the interpretation of their dreams, they would accept Yusuf's call, although this interpretation was of a very particular kind.

﴿Indeed, I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who deny the Hereafter.﴾ "Indeed, I have abandoned the way of a people who do not believe in Allah and who deny the Hereafter."

This also points to the people among whom he was raised, namely the household of the Chief of Egypt and the courtiers of the king of Egypt, and to the whole nation that obeyed the king of Egypt. Although these two young men were, obviously, upon the religion of the king and of their own people, yet in speaking with them Prophet Yusuf does not say, "I have left your religion," but speaks in a general manner, so that hatred of the religion of Islam would not arise in the hearts of these young men. This is extremely wise and a supremely excellent method of preaching, and a manner of conveying the message with the utmost delicacy and insight.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 38:

Having pointed out the signs of disbelief, Yusuf (peace be upon him) places before these young men the signs of faith, which he and his forefathers follow.

"I have followed the way of my forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. It is not for us to associate anything with Allah."

The Islamic millah (community of faith) is a millah of complete tawhid (monotheism), and there is not even a trace of shirk (associating partners with Allah) in it. Guidance to tawhid is a favour and grace from Allah. And this favour and grace is so general that every person can accept it and attain it, because its inclination and its principles are present within human nature (fitrah). Its indications and proofs are also present within the human environment. Its teachings are also present in the guidance of the Messengers and in the heavenly Books. Yet the condition of people is that they are depriving themselves of this general favour and grace.

﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most people do not give thanks.﴾ (Yusuf 12:38)

Yusuf is gradually planting his message in their hearts, with great caution and great gentleness. He keeps lodging the matter in their hearts and gradually expresses his beliefs and convictions, while also making clear that your beliefs and those of your people are wrong, false and baseless, and that as a consequence the society in which you live is a corrupt society. After this lengthy preface, Yusuf now states the real matter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 39:

Yusuf (peace be upon him), in these very brief, clear and decisive words, has laid down all the signposts of the path of the religion of Islam. All the constituent elements of this religion have been stated. Yusuf does not directly invite them to these signposts and elements, but places them before them as a subject for reflection.

يٰصَاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ ءَاَرْبَابٌ مُّتَفَرِّقُوْنَ خَيْرٌ اَمِ اللّٰهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ: "O my two fellow prisoners, is it better that there be many scattered lords, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?"

This is a question that goes directly to the depths of human nature and strongly shakes the human disposition. It is the demand of human nature that there should be one God. If you feel that this is the demand of nature, then why do you believe in many scattered lords? That is, the being who deserves to be recognised as Lord and Ruler, who should be worshipped, served and obeyed continuously, is only Allah, the One and the Irresistible. If we accept that the God and Lord of human nature and the nature of the universe is Allah alone, then it necessarily follows that in the practical life of man, the Lord, the Commander and the Legislator should be Allah alone. And it is not possible that people should know that Allah alone is the Creator and the Subduer, and yet still worship and obey other than Allah, and have someone other than Him as their ruler. The Lord is indeed the God and the Ruler. He also manages the affairs of this entire universe, and it is not possible that a being which cannot manage the universe should be the Lord of mankind; this is rationally impossible.

Therefore, Allah, the One and the Irresistible, alone is deserving of this, and it is better that people worship Him, instead of worshipping scattered lords whom blind ignorance has fashioned, whose vision is short, and who can see nothing but deception. The greatest misfortune for humanity is that it accepts many gods instead of one God, and that these many gods tear its life into pieces. Even within their inclinations and tendencies there is conflict. The lords other than Allah that we have made are, in reality, laying hands on the sovereignty right of Allah the Exalted. And because of our ignorance, our superstition, and our myths and tales, we have accepted these lords besides Allah as Lord. Or some tyrannical and dominating human gods have imposed their system of lordship on people by force. These human lords cannot, even for a single moment, be separated from their personal interests, their own existence, and the feelings and desires for the preservation of their honour. And in their hearts the desire that their domination over the common people continue and remain is filled to the brim. The policy and permanent policy of such gods is that they crush to pieces those forces from which they fear any harm, directly or indirectly. Moreover, these gods always keep alive those forces, nurture them, and carry out propaganda in their favour, which help in the establishment and continuance of their divinity. These gods are always busy in the advancement and honouring of all such institutions.

Whereas Allah is the One and the Irresistible, and He is free of both needs. Allah's demand from people is only that they fear Allah, take the path of goodness, and reform themselves and their environment, and that this reform and constructive work be in accordance with the Shariah established by Allah. If they do so, then all their work will also be entirely worship. The acts of worship that Allah has made obligatory for humans are also such that the reform of human hearts, minds, character and conduct itself is intended through them. Otherwise, Allah has no need at all for any worship or servitude from people.

يا أيها الناس أنتم الفقراء إلى الله والله هو الغني الحميد: "O people, you are in need of Allah, and Allah alone is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy." Therefore, there is a great difference between the worship and servitude of Allah, and the worship and servitude of other gods besides Allah.

Thereafter Yusuf (peace be upon him) takes one step further, and now he openly criticizes the ideas and illusions of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam): "You worship besides Him nothing but names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgement belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know." (Qur'an 12:40)

These lords, whether they are from among humans or non-human beings, such as angels, spirits, devils, or other cosmic forces subject to Allah, are in no sense lords. They possess no share of the reality of lordship, because the right of lordship and the station of lordship belong to Allah alone, and He alone is deserving of it. He is the Creator, and under His control all creatures continue to live. But in various jahiliyyahs, people have themselves named certain powers as "lord" of their own accord. They attribute the attributes of the true Lord to these so-called lords, although in reality these lords possess neither those attributes, nor do they have the power of dominance and subjugation over anyone as the true Lord does.

Now Yusuf (peace be upon him) delivers the final blow against their false beliefs and shows who is the true holder of sovereignty. Who is entitled to be obeyed? Who deserves to be worshipped, and worshipped alone?

"Judgement belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know." (Qur'an 12:40)

Sovereignty and rule belong to Allah alone; sovereignty is an exclusive attribute of divinity. Therefore no other ruler can exist besides Allah. If any person other than Allah lays claim to this right of Allah, his case will be with Allah, whether the one claiming sovereignty besides Allah is a single individual, a class, a group, a nation, all people, or an international institution. Whoever claims sovereignty in opposition to Allah commits kufr, and this is clear disbelief on his part. This verse is an explicit text upon it.

How can anyone claim divinity in opposition to Allah? In any form, if someone makes such a claim, the claimant is a disbeliever and outside the fold of Islam, whether he claims as Pharaoh did and says, "I am your lord, the Most High" (Qur'an 79:24), or says, "I know of no god for you other than myself" (Qur'an 28:38), or he removes the Islamic Shari'ah from the system of governance, or he decides that the source of rule and legislation will be someone other than Allah, whether he is an individual or a collective of people.

In the Islamic system, the Muslim community selects the ruler and entrusts a person with authority, and he exercises these powers, but he may use his powers only within the limits of the Shari'ah. In the Islamic system, no person or institution is the source of legislation or the source of sovereignty; the authority of sovereignty and legislation belongs to Allah alone. Countless Muslim thinkers do not distinguish between the exercise of the right of sovereignty and the source of sovereignty. The actual reality is that not all humans possess the right of sovereignty; the right of sovereignty belongs to Allah alone. As for humans, their duty is only to implement the system of law and constitution which Allah has prescribed; humans are merely its implementers. But any constitution and law which Allah has not made has no legal standing, and its legal standing is nothing at all.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) is also presenting the proof of this matter. We can understand this proof only when we properly grasp the meaning of the word 'ibadah (worship), in the sense in which the Arabs understood it.

The meaning of 'abd in Arabic is (dan, khada', dhall): that is, to become subservient, to become obedient to a command, and to bow and humble oneself before someone. At the dawn of Islam, the meaning of 'ibadah was also not the observance of ritual servitude and worship, because when these verses were first revealed, the rituals of servitude had not yet been made obligatory. These (salah, sawm, hajj, zakah and jihad) were made obligatory later. Initially the word 'ibadah was used in its lexical meaning, which later came to be used in its technical meaning. Initially the meaning of this word was that only Allah should be obeyed, only before Allah should one bow, only Allah's commands should be accepted; whether these commands related to the rituals of worship or to moral matters, the word 'ibadah applied to all these spheres. Its meaning included obedience and servitude, concerning which Allah commanded that no one else be obeyed or served.

When we understand this meaning of 'ibadah, then it becomes clear to us that Yusuf (peace be upon him) said that the command belongs to Allah, so worship, servitude and obedience are also to Him alone. If the command belongs to someone else, then the concept of serving Allah alone cannot even be conceived. And the statement that the command belongs to Allah is a general principle: it refers to the creative command as well, that He alone disposes of affairs in this universe, and it refers to the legislative and legal sovereignty too, that religious and creative affairs also belong to Allah alone.

I repeat this point: whoever claims sovereignty in opposition to Allah in matters of rule has left the religion of Islam. The ruling of Islam about him is clear and binding, and this is in fact the worst shirk and clear kufr (kufr bawah). Likewise, those who acknowledge a person who claims sovereignty in opposition to Allah, obey him wholeheartedly, and feel no discomfort in their hearts, they too are committers of kufr bawah and are outside the religion of Islam.

Yusuf says that since Allah alone is the absolute ruler, therefore Allah alone is deserving of obedience, and this is the correct and right religion: "That is the upright religion" (dhalika al-din al-qayyim), meaning there is no other form of the upright religion. The correct religion is that in which sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, and the manifestation of Allah's sovereignty is such that people worship and obey Allah alone.

Since people do not know the reality, it does not follow that, because of their ignorance, they are considered to be upon the upright religion. For how can the existence of religion be realized in the life of one who does not even know Islam? If the condition of people is that they are unaware of the reality of religion itself, then rationally, and as a matter of fact, it cannot be said that they are upon religion. Ignorance is no excuse that could endow them with the quality of Islam, because ignorance negates altogether the quality of religion, since no one can hold belief in Islam unless he knows Islam. This point is extremely logical and self-evident.

Through these clear, decisive and concise words, Yusuf has cut the root of shirk and laid down the true marks of the religion of Islam. Here he has stated all the fundamental elements of the Islamic worldview, and in a couple of sentences he has cut the root of jahiliyyah.

In the world, a taghut system is established only when it snatches the right of sovereignty from Allah and makes people obey it instead of Allah. That is, people become obedient to its laws and not to the Shari'ah and law of Allah, and it introduces its own taghut thinking, taghut laws, taghut commands and obedience. Taghut is not established in any other way.

A taghut system is established only when the religion of Islam disappears from the world. When the belief becomes firmly rooted in people's hearts and minds that there is no other sovereign or authority besides Allah, and that in all matters of life humans must obey Allah alone, then at that time a taghut system cannot be established.

Here Yusuf concludes his true lesson and instruction, and he had linked this discourse, at the beginning of the account, with the purpose and meaning of the prisoners. That is why we now return to our main subject, so as to also answer the question of the prisoners.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 41:

Yusuf did not specify here who would reach a good end and who would reach a bad end, because he did not consider it appropriate to address the one who would meet a bad end personally. However, he emphasised it by saying that the outcome would indeed be this. This matter is decided, and just as the decision is made, so it will come to pass. Yusuf was a prisoner who had committed no crime. The king had ordered his imprisonment without reflection or investigation. Perhaps the courtiers around him presented the incident of the wife of the Egyptian nobleman in such a way that Yusuf was portrayed as guilty, as influential circles generally do. Therefore, on this occasion, Yusuf considered it appropriate to convey to the king that he should investigate his case.

The meaning is: to mention my condition, my story and my reality before your Lord and ruler, to whose legal and constitutional system you are subject, and whose commands you obey. In this sense He is your Lord, because the meaning of "rabb" is none other than one who is ruler, chief and lawgiver. The concept of lordship (rububiyyah) in the Islamic terminology is made clear here. It should be kept in view that Prophet Yusuf was in the age of shepherd kings, and the shepherd kings did not hold the belief that they themselves were lords, as the Pharaohs held. Nor did they consider themselves gods like the Pharaohs. For them, the meaning of lordship was sovereignty; here the word "rabb" is clearly used in the sense of ruler.

Now the context does not give the details that the fate of the fellow prisoners was exactly as Prophet Yusuf had interpreted the dream. Here the story leaves a gap, and the readers themselves understand that it happened so. But the person about whom Prophet Yusuf's interpretation was that he would be saved did not fulfil Prophet Yusuf's bequest concerning him. When he returned to the bustle of royal palace life, he became intoxicated with those activities; he also forgot the lesson of tawhid, and did not even present the matter of Prophet Yusuf.

Fa-labitha: this final pronoun (labth) refers back to Prophet Yusuf. It was the wisdom of Allah's will that Prophet Yusuf should be cut off from all worldly means and rely only upon Allah. In the view of the divine will, it was not befitting to Prophet Yusuf's station that his release should come through a worldly and human means.

It is the duty of the sincere servants of Allah to become purely devoted to Allah. They should call upon Him alone in their needs and supplicate that Allah keep them firm. And if at any time these servants fall short, then Allah's grace comes upon them, and they are set back upon their true path. They proceed again upon the way of Allah with fresh longing, love and contentment, and His grace and favour are fully completed upon them.

The scene then shifts again, and we arrive at the king's court. The king has seen a significant dream. He asks his courtiers, his soothsayers and his religious leaders for its true interpretation.

The king sought the interpretation of the dream, but the courtiers who sat around him, and the religious leaders of the court, could not tell its interpretation. Either they did sense that the country was going to face some difficulties, but they did not dare to express any ill omen in front of the king. It is the method of court officials that they either brush the matter aside, or ignore whatever they cannot understand. Accordingly, they commented on these significant dreams in just this way: that these are confused dreams, and they see no understanding of their interpretation, because there is no clear indication in these dreams.

Up to this point we have encountered three dreams: the dream of Hadrat Yusuf, the dreams of Yusuf's two fellow prisoners, and the dream of the king of the time. From these dreams, and their interpretations, it becomes clear that in that era, in Egypt and in the surrounding world beyond Egypt, the art of dream interpretation was flourishing greatly, and the ability Allah gave Hadrat Yusuf from His side, that he could reach the interpretation of dreams, was a perfection that was the spirit of the age. And whatever miracles are given to all the prophets, they are in keeping with their contemporary environment. So, was the interpretation of dreams a miracle for Hadrat Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam)? In Fi Zilal al-Quran we do not open debates on this point. In any case, the king has seen a dream and there is a search for its interpretation.

The scene then shifts again, and we arrive at the king's court. The king has seen a significant dream. He asks his courtiers, his soothsayers and his religious leaders for its true interpretation.

The king sought the interpretation of the dream, but the courtiers who sat around him, and the religious leaders of the court, could not tell its interpretation. Either they did sense that the country was going to face some difficulties, but they did not dare to express any ill omen in front of the king. It is the method of court officials that they either brush the matter aside, or ignore whatever they cannot understand. Accordingly, they commented on these significant dreams in just this way: that these are confused dreams, and they see no understanding of their interpretation, because there is no clear indication in these dreams.

Up to this point we have encountered three dreams: the dream of Hadrat Yusuf, the dreams of Yusuf's two fellow prisoners, and the dream of the king of the time. From these dreams, and their interpretations, it becomes clear that in that era, in Egypt and in the surrounding world beyond Egypt, the art of dream interpretation was flourishing greatly, and the ability Allah gave Hadrat Yusuf from His side, that he could reach the interpretation of dreams, was a perfection that was the spirit of the age. And whatever miracles are given to all the prophets, they are in keeping with their contemporary environment. So, was the interpretation of dreams a miracle for Hadrat Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam)? In Fi Zilal al-Quran we do not open debates on this point. In any case, the king has seen a dream and there is a search for its interpretation.

The surviving prisoner, his companion, now remembers Yusuf. Before this, Shaytan had caused him to forget Yusuf, and this man had become occupied with the bustle of the palace, with guests, with wine, and with pleasure and revelry. Now he recalls Yusuf, who had earlier given the interpretation of his dream, and it had appeared exactly as a reality.

This man says: "I will tell you its interpretation, so send me forth." Now, at this point, the curtain falls and this scene comes to an end. When the curtain rises, we hear the dialogue of Yusuf in the prison (the following verses).

Here, this man uses the word "Siddiq" for Yusuf, meaning one who speaks the truth abundantly. He uses this word because he has seen that the Prophet is a Siddiq of the highest rank. And then he relates the king's dream: "Aftina..."

This man relates the words of the dream exactly as they were, because he seeks its interpretation. Therefore it is necessary to tell the whole dream. So he relates the dream word for word.

Here Joseph explains the dream's interpretation and also gives advice and counsel.

He said: "For seven consecutive years you will keep sowing and cultivating, one after another without interruption. These will be green and flourishing years, and the allusion to them was in the words 'seven fat cows' (baqarat samān)."

"Then, during these years, whatever crops you harvest, store the grain in its ears, leaving only a small portion, the amount that will serve for your food." That is, in these years, leave the crop you reap inside its ears so that it remains safe from insects of the earth and other weather effects. Yes, what you are going to use, thresh and clean, but the portion used should be small, so that as much grain as possible is saved for the time of hardship.

These seven years will be so harsh that there will be no agricultural produce during them. These years will consume everything. The purpose of this is that these years will be years of famine, and only what you have stored in the preceding years will remain from them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 49:

Now these seven dry years will end, your previously stored grain will also run out, and a period of greenery and abundance will return. Rains will fall, water and crops will increase, the grape harvest will be abundant, and people will extract its juice and make wine. Likewise there will be sesame, olives, and other oil-bearing fruits and seeds. It should be kept in view here that the dream of the king contains no indication of this period of prosperity after the seven years of drought. Rather, Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) is saying this by virtue of his knowledge granted directly by Allah (ladunni) and his prophetic knowledge. Thus Prophet Yusuf gave the royal envoy the good news that after the seven difficult years, a period of widespread prosperity would come, so that he might inform the king of it.

Now we are once again in the royal court, and a different scene appears before us; between these two scenes there is a gap, which the human imagination fills by itself. Here the royal messenger has given a complete report. The interpretation of the dream has been explained, and he has also told the king about the unjust punishment of Yusuf. But these matters are not mentioned in the context of the discourse. Before us comes the king's desire.

﴿وَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ ائْتُوْنِيْ بِهٖ﴾: The king said, "Bring him to me."

Further details are set aside. The king's command is issued. A messenger goes directly to Yusuf, but Yusuf sends the messenger back. We do not know whether this messenger is the same cupbearer or someone else. The execution of royal orders may have been entrusted to someone else. But Yusuf, even after a long imprisonment, does not hasten to leave the prison. He wishes that his case be decided rightly, that truth be established, that the schemes of the wrongdoers be exposed, and that he be cleared and leave with honour. This peace of heart and this tranquillity can come only as the result of divine training. Now he has become so mature that there is no trace of haste in his temperament.

Yusuf's seriousness, maturity and tranquillity are clear in both positions. In the first, he told the cupbearer only, "Mention me to your lord." In the second, despite the royal order for his release, he said, "First investigate the case of my affair." But there is a difference between the first position and the second, because several years of imprisonment and training have made him even more mature.

Yusuf rejected the royal order of release so that the king might properly know what the reality of his affair is, and what the reality of the charges of those women is. By pointing to the incident of the women, he in effect said that when an investigation is held, the women who cut their hands can tell the actual situation. This investigation should be held in Yusuf's absence, so that Yusuf's presence in the royal court does not affect an impartial investigation. All of this is because Yusuf was certain of his innocence and was confident that the outcome would certainly be in his favour, for truth cannot remain hidden, nor can it be concealed for long.

The Qur'an has caused Yusuf (peace be upon him) to use the word "Rabb" and has joined it to the addressee (rabbika). This is because Yusuf's Lord is Allah, whereas the Lord of that messenger is the king, whose servant he is in the governing system; from this there emerges the meaning that the ruler is also regarded as a lord.

Now the messenger returns and gives his report, but the Qur'an passes over the intervening links, leaving them to human imagination, and moves on. The scene of the inquiry assembly:

﴿He said: "What was your business when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said: "Far be God from it! We know no evil in him." The chief's wife said: "Now the truth has come to light. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and he is indeed of the truthful."﴾

Upon this, the king asked those women: what was your experience at the time you tried to entice Joseph?

This shows what went on in the house of the chief of Egypt. Moreover, the conversation the women had in their own gathering has already been recorded earlier. It also shows that whenever a people enjoys prosperity, moral degradation of this kind arises among the women of its upper classes, even where their environment is backward. The ignorance under discussion belongs to ancient history, but ignorance, in whatever era it occurs, is ignorance, its features are the same everywhere, and its prosperous classes sink into wickedness and debauchery.

Now, in the inquiry held in the royal court, these women had no room to fabricate another lie.

﴿They all said with one voice: "Far be God from it! We found no evil in him."﴾ They said, "Ḥāshā lillāh" (Far be God from it), all together, and that we found in him not even a trace of evil.

This was the truth, and now it was difficult for them. These women were extremely shameless and bold, but the matter was so clear that there was no way left to deny it.

Now the woman who was infatuated with Joseph comes forward, the one who had been unable to sever her attachment to him after he had rejected her. This woman comes forward, plainly confesses her guilt, and gives the good news of Joseph's innocence.

﴿The chief's wife said: "Now the truth has come to light. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and he is indeed of the truthful."﴾ The chief's wife spoke up: "Now the truth has become clear. It was I who tried to seduce him, and he is certainly among the truthful."

Now the cat is out of the bag. The truth has come to light. It was I who tried to entice him.

"Innā rāwadtuhu ʿan nafsihi wa innahu la-mina al-ṣādiqīn": It was I who tried to seduce him, and indeed he is among the truthful. The manner in which she bears witness shows that she still hoped to win Joseph's sympathy. It is also possible that Joseph's beliefs and ideas had taken root in her heart and she had come to believe. That is why she says: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in secret, and that God does not guide the stratagem of the betrayers.﴾ That is, so that the chief of Egypt may know that I did not betray him in private, and that God does not set on the path of success the schemes of those who betray.

The commentary on this verse is written so that, within its context, a storm of emotion is visible behind it, just as earlier she made a clear confession, and in a very beautiful manner.

﴿Ana raawadtuhu 'an nafsihi wa innahu laminas-saadiqeen﴾: "It was I who tried to seduce him, and he is indeed truthful." This was a clear testimony to the chastity and complete courage of Hadrat Yusuf. She gave this testimony with great boldness and paid no heed to what effects it would have upon her own person.

Did this woman give testimony before the king and his courtiers solely for the sake of truth? Yes, but there is certainly another purpose and desire in her heart as well: that this believing man, whom she had tried to seduce for physical ends, should now respect her for this testimony and acknowledgement. For, after he had been absent in prison, she had come to faith. This is the meaning.

﴿Dhalika li-ya'lama annee lam akhunhu bil-ghayb﴾: "That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence."

After this, the woman makes a further effort to correct the situation, saying:

﴿Wa innallaha la yahdee kaydal-khaaaineen﴾: "Allah does not let the plotting of the treacherous succeed." That is, she acknowledges the reality that Hadrat Yusuf would like to hear.

She goes one step further:

﴿Wa maa ubarri'u nafsee, inna an-nafsa la-ammaaratum bis-soo'i illaa maa rahima rabbee, inna rabbee ghafoorun raheem﴾: "I do not claim my soul to be free (of blame); indeed the soul is certainly inclined to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed my Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

This woman was a loving one. In the age of ignorance she bore an ignorant love for that person, and now in Islam too she loves him. Therefore her utmost endeavour is to somehow obtain from Hadrat Yusuf some word of goodness, or attention, or joy.

This is the element of human emotion in this story. It has not been brought here merely for artistry. It has been brought here solely for lesson and admonition, so that through it ideas and beliefs may be spread and the Islamic call may be extended. Wherever human emotions, inclinations, and human imagination and intuition have been introduced into this story, they have been introduced in a manner that is very gentle, full of love, and beautiful, in a way that harmonizes with all the influences, all the events, all the characters and the environment, and so that the environment being indicated appears natural.

Here the hardships of Hadrat Yusuf's period of captivity come to an end. Now Hadrat Yusuf will be tested by being given honour and authority. For a human being, every condition is a test.

Here this part (juz') concludes, and further events may be seen in the next part.

**Para 13 at a Glance**

This para consists of the remaining part of Surah Yusuf, together with Surah Ar-Ra'd and Surah Ibrahim. Both of these surahs are also Makkan. The whole para is therefore Makkan Qur'an and contains all the characteristics of Makkan surahs.

We will leave the commentary on Surah Ar-Ra'd and Surah Ibrahim until later. As for Surah Yusuf, we hope readers will keep in mind the commentary on Surah Yusuf made in the previous para before studying its remaining part.

This para contains the rest of Surah Yusuf, with commentary scattered throughout it, and at the end a commentary on the whole surah. In this part we become acquainted with some new aspects of the personal life and character of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), the central figure of the story. Alongside the basic constituent elements of his personality, which we mentioned while describing the characters of this story, some new aspects of his personality come to the fore in this new stage. This personality has the same features from beginning to end, but in this new stage some new qualities appear, and these new characteristics apparently seem to be new.

The personality of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), through his development, his speech, the events, and the difficulties that came upon him, is now a complete personality. This completion of personality takes place under purely divine training, as a result of which he emerges as a righteous servant. This servant is being prepared precisely so that he may attain establishment in the land and so that he may receive authority in a country of the Middle East from which goods are supplied in every direction.

What are the new features of this personality? First, his bond with Allah is very deep, and he is content with His decree. He has become Allah's own, and he has complete trust in Allah. He has cast off all worldly values and has been freed from all the bonds of the earth. He is independent of the rulers of this world. These worldly values and these powers have no significance in the eyes of this personality, because this personality has now attached its heart to Allah alone.

These qualities of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) come to the fore at the time when the emissaries of the king of Egypt come to him in the prison and express the wish that the king wishes to meet him. Yet Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) does not lose himself on this occasion. Nor does he show any impatience to leave the darkness of the prison and meet the king of the time, although on such occasions impatience and haste are usually shown, especially when a person is confined in a prison cell.

This change in the character of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) can be understood only when we look back at the circumstances a few years earlier.
