A few years earlier, he himself had asked the man who was going to be released to present his case before the king. It is clearly seen that in this way the values of this personality have changed. His faith is still present as before, but now there is a tranquility in his personality. He is still content with Allah's decree and is walking along with that decree. He sees how decree does its work. He has that assurance which his great forefather had sought, who said to God: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." The Lord said: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes, but I seek the satisfaction of my heart."

This is the tranquility that divine training has poured into the heart of this chosen servant. By putting him through trials, placing him in difficulties, passing him through various circumstances and observations, and granting him knowledge, insight, certainty, and tranquility, he has reached this station.

After this stage, this quality is very clear in the character of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him). The final commentaries on this surah come here. When he is in intimate supplication with his Lord, he is not independent of worldly values. He says:

﴿My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Creator of the heavens and the earth, You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾ (101)

Now as for the prejudices and commentaries that have come in this surah, we have said a great deal about them, and further explanations will come in the commentary on the verses. Here, the only purpose was to mention the change that arose in the personality of this chosen servant, who plays a great role in this story. Along with this change, his personality is now a complete personality. Moreover, this is the quality that is intended to be highlighted in this whole section, because Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) is to carry out the work of reviving Islam, and this is the method of revolution of the Qur'an: it establishes the real objective in the minds of its readers.

Now we come to the explanation and commentary of the verses.

**Lesson 109 at a Glance**

In this lesson the story of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) moves forward. This is the fourth scene of the four major scenes of this story. In the previous para, the three links of this story were completed. Now Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) has come out of the prison. The king himself has requested that he is about to entrust him with an important office. The responsibilities of this new office are discussed here.

This lesson begins with the final sentence of the previous scene. The final link of the previous scene was that in it, at the request of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), the king conducted an inquiry about Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) from the women who had cut their hands. The purpose was that the causes which had led to Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) being unjustly imprisoned should become clear, so that his innocence would be announced. This matter was necessary for his new office, so that he might carry out his new responsibilities with complete composure, full conviction, and confidence. His soul should be at rest, and he should carry out the affairs of the state with confidence. His life of calling now consisted of two kinds of activity: the responsibilities of the state and the responsibilities of the Islamic call. Therefore, it was appropriate that in this period of double responsibilities he should emerge, having shaken off the dust of the past and become light.

His nobility was that at this stage he said nothing about the wife of the ruler of Egypt, not even giving any hint of her. He only said that the king should investigate the matter of the women who had cut their hands. But the wife of the ruler of Egypt herself came forward and declared what the truth was and what had happened:

﴿He said, "What was your business when you sought to seduce Yusuf?" They said, "Perfect is Allah! We know of him no evil." The wife of the ruler said, "Now the truth has become manifest; it was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed, he is of the truthful. [He said], 'That is so that he will know that I did not betray him in his absence and that Allah does not guide the plan of betrayers. And I do not [claim to] acquit myself; indeed, the soul is incessantly commanding [to evil], except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.'"﴾ (Yusuf 51–53)

Here the sorrowful past of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) comes to an end, and now the stage of prosperity, honour, and authority begins.

**Verses 53 to 57**

﴿Thus did We establish Yusuf in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We cause whom We will to reach Our mercy, and We do not allow to be lost the reward of the doers of good. And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were fearing Allah.﴾

Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) achieved his innocence in the king's court, and at the same time he came to know the true interpretation of his dream. The king also saw how Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) had arranged the investigation of the women's affair. Moreover, his nobility and self-respect were also clearly proved before the king, that this man does not even consider coming out of the prison without being declared innocent, nor is he eager to meet the king. The king was also no ordinary king but the king of a great country like Egypt. On this occasion he adopted the stance of a most noble and generous person, who, even with an accusation hanging over him, does not consent to come out of prison. He wishes, before seeking positions, meeting the king, or facing the hardships of prison, to remove the stain from his honour and reputation, and he wishes to do this before setting foot in the king's court. All these matters increased the king's regard and importance for him in his heart, so he said:

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself."﴾ (12:54)

The king of the time did not summon Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) merely for release, nor merely because he was an expert in psychology and the interpretation of dreams, nor to inform him of the king's consent so that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) would be overjoyed. He summoned him not for these purposes, but so that he might be his special adviser, his personal friend, and a trusted man.

We feel pity for those people who sacrifice their honour and nobility at the thresholds of kings. These people are free and blameless, yet they themselves take the yoke of slavery in their hands and place it around their necks. They seek the pleasure of their elders, or are delighted to hear a word of praise from them, and then remain most obedient servants. Rather, they humble themselves and bow before their elders. If only such people would read Surah Yusuf and learn what the taste of self-respect, dignity, nobility, and seriousness is. Yet the benefits of self-respect, dignity, and honour are greater than the life of flattery, slavery, and humiliation. In any case, the king issued this order.

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself."﴾ (12:54)

Now, in the context of the speech here, the links such as Prophet Yusuf's (peace be upon him) release have been omitted and left to the human imagination.

﴿So when he spoke to him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted with us."﴾ (12:54) When Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) spoke with the king, the king came to know that the signs which Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) displayed were consistent with his truthfulness, so the king announced that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) now held a station of honour in his realm. Now Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) was no longer a Hebrew slave, nor was he an accused person ensnared by the charge the wife of the ruler of Egypt had laid against him. Now he was a person of honour, held in high rank by the king, and he was a most trustworthy man.

After this announcement by the king, what was Prophet Yusuf's (peace be upon him) conduct? He did not perform a prostration of gratitude before the king, as courtiers usually do before kings. Nor did he say, with flattery and servility, "O my master, may you live long, and this servant will remain your servant," or that he was their trustee, servant, and slave. Rather, instead of flattery and servility, he plainly stated that he was ready to render whatever services he could in the difficulties that would confront the realm, in accordance with the circumstances to come, which would necessarily follow from the interpretation of the dream. For Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) had firm certainty that only he was seeing the coming difficulties, and only he could make preparations and precautions for them, otherwise people would go into the jaws of death through famine. Only Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) could save the country through his trustworthiness and integrity.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 54–55 (part 1 of 3):

He said, "Make me in charge of the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I am a guardian who has knowledge." (12:55) Yusuf (peace be upon him) said, "Place the treasuries of the kingdom under my control. I am both a guardian and a knowledgeable person."

The summary of the coming task is that there are seven years of abundance, and in them there is a need to save a portion of the produce ..... , to run the affairs of the state in a good manner, to set right all the departments of the state, and to plan during the period of prosperity in such a way that it can be benefited from in times of hardship and drought. For this reason, Yusuf (peace be upon him) mentioned precisely those qualities that were necessary for such circumstances, namely ḥafīẓ and ʿalīm. This arrangement was beneficial for Egypt and all the surrounding regions and countries. Therefore he said, ﴿Indeed, I am a guardian who has knowledge﴾ (12:55). Yusuf's (peace be upon him) demand was not made so that he might take the ministry of finance and obtain some benefits for himself; rather, he was a man of sound judgment and an intellectual, and he considered that no one else was more suitable for this duty than himself. The coming period would be a period of famine, because the entire Egyptian nation and neighbouring peoples would face the great problem of arranging for grain and other provisions. In the seven good years there was the great task of economy, and in the seven difficult years there was the great task of maintaining supply. Yusuf (peace be upon him) did not ask for anything for his own person; rather, this was that great responsibility from which everyone was fleeing, and no one was ready to accept it gladly, considering it a windfall. Firstly, in the royal system there was the danger of being executed; secondly, it is not possible to control the common people in a state of hunger and destitution, because when the people are hungry they tear apart the officials like madmen. All these possibilities were before Yusuf (peace be upon him).

Here a doubt arises: that what Yusuf (peace be upon him) said and demanded, "Appoint me over the treasures of the earth, for I am a guardian and knowledgeable," is it not a demand for an office, which is severely disapproved of in the Islamic system? Since this is an explicit demand to be appointed to a post, and the hadith states: "By God, we do not entrust this matter to the one who asks for it" (agreed upon).

The second objection is that Yusuf (peace be upon him) himself here stated that he is a guardian and knowledgeable. This is in some sense a declaration of self-purification, and the Qur'an itself says: ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ ("Do not claim purity of your own selves"). The easy answer to this may be that these administrative principles were implemented in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, but it is not necessary that they were forbidden in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him) as well, because while there has been agreement among all the prophets on the principles of religion, administrative matters and legal rulings have differed from one to another.

But we do not give this as a superficial answer, because this matter needs to be examined with some depth, and its results are very profound and far-reaching. It has some further aspects and considerations, and it is necessary to view it from these angles in a broad perspective, so that in deriving the rulings of jurisprudence we may derive matters from this broad point of view and give a dynamic approach to the jurisprudential rulings as well. Because jurisprudential rulings, their methodology of derivation and the principles of jurisprudence have also become frozen during the period of stagnation and decline of the Muslims. They too need to be given a dynamic, movement-oriented approach.

The truth is that Islamic jurisprudence did not come into existence in a vacuum, nor can it be understood or implemented in a vacuum. The development of Islamic jurisprudence took place within a developing Islamic society. That society, in its developmental period, had to fulfil the needs of Islamic life. It was not Islamic jurisprudence that gave birth to an Islamic society; rather, within an Islamic society, Islamic jurisprudence developed to meet its needs. These are two great facts, and Islamic history bears witness to them. Unless we understand the relationship between the Islamic society and the formation of jurisprudence, we cannot understand Islamic jurisprudence, nor can we understand its dynamic and developmental status.

Those who today read these texts and take the codified rulings of jurisprudence, and who do not keep in view the fact that first an Islamic society came into existence and then jurisprudence came into existence, and who also do not look at the circumstances in which these texts were revealed, and how the Islamic jurisprudential issues were compiled, especially do not keep in view the environment, the society and the temperament in which these texts were revealed, such people want to implement this law in a vacuum, whereas no legal system is ever implemented in a vacuum; rather it is implemented in a society. Such people are in reality not jurists, nor are they experts in Islamic law. These people have in fact not understood the temperament of the Islamic system, nor the reality of this religion.

Dynamic jurisprudence is in fact different from the jurisprudence that exists in the pages of books, although dynamic jurisprudence too is based on the same principles and texts on which the jurisprudence of the pages is based. Dynamic jurisprudence also keeps in view the circumstances in which the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah were revealed. A practical jurist sees that the occasion of revelation and the circumstances of revelation cannot be separated from the original texts. If we consider a text in isolation from the circumstances in which it was revealed, our deduction and ijtihad will become wrong, and the jurisprudence formed in this way will not be correct.

This is why no divine jurisprudential command is such that it came on its own in a vacuum, without the influence of the environment and society in which it first appeared. No jurisprudential ruling or ijtihad has occurred in a vacuum, so it cannot remain in a vacuum.

Examples of the principle we have stated above are those rulings in which it is said that a person should not claim his own purity or should not present himself for an office. These rulings are derived from the verse ﴿So do not claim purity of your own selves﴾ and from the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "By God, we do not give this office to the one who asks for it."

These rulings came in a society which was an Islamic society, and in that Islamic society these rulings were in fact actually implemented. These rulings were meant for precisely such a society, so that they might fulfil the needs of an established Islamic society. The Islamic society of that time had its own historical background and its own particular organic structure; that society had its own specific and personal situation. These two rulings were such rulings as were to be implemented within a fully established Islamic society, and it was in precisely those circumstances that they were revealed. They were not revealed in a vacuum. Therefore we can implement these two rulings within an established Islamic society, a society whose composition, whose upbringing and whose organic movement is Islamic. Whenever such a society is established, such rulings and a system in accordance with them will be established within it. If there is no trace of an Islamic society anywhere, these rulings cannot be implemented in it, in a vacuum.

The same is the case with all Islamic rulings, but we do not think it appropriate here to give details about the other Islamic rulings.

The question is: why would people in an Islamic society not make themselves into a "Mithu" by praising themselves, and why would they not put themselves forward as candidates, and why would they not be able to campaign for their preferred individuals so that they may be selected for the Shura council, as governor, or for some other office?

The truth is that when an Islamic society is established, people will have no need for any propaganda to express their ability and merit. Moreover, in an Islamic society, office is a kind of responsibility, and only a fool would strive to take upon himself a responsibility without reason. The only exception is that one may desire such an office for the sake of seeking the pleasure of Allah, earning reward through serving humanity, or performing duties within society; but even then, it is only in the manner that someone places that office and responsibility upon him. Those who themselves make demands and run after offices are light-minded people, and their purpose in those offices is to obtain other objectives. Therefore it is necessary that such people are never offered these offices.

But this truth can be understood only when the establishment of an Islamic society and its temperament are understood, and its nature of formation is in mind. The truth is that movement and motion are the very life of any Islamic society. An Islamic society in fact comes into existence as a result of an Islamic movement. How? 

(1) For example, a message and a belief are sent down from Allah. A Messenger conveys it. In the time of prophethood, the Messenger himself used to convey it; after the period of prophethood, however, a caller in place of the Messenger calls to this same belief. Some people accept this call, whereas in the early days of the call the system of government is jahili, and this jahili system of government and this jahili society persecute the movement. In the period of trial, affliction and tribulation, some people abandon the movement and apostatise, while some stand firm and are martyred, and others wait and continue the work.

Those who bear difficulties and continue the work, Allah grants them victory. These people then become the instrument of the hand of power; Allah grants them establishment on earth, dominance and authority, because this is His permanent promise. In this way these people establish the rule of God on earth and implement the commands of Allah in it. This authority and establishment on earth is not for the sake of these people themselves; rather, this support and dominance is for the religion of Allah and to establish on earth the system of Allah's lordship.

This vanguard of the religion, carrying the religion, does not stop at any earthly boundary, nor does it confine itself within the bounds of any nation or lineage. It is not confined to any colour or lineage, nor to any language or form; these are very weak and unstable elements and limited circles. Rather, this vanguard, carrying this message, spreads throughout the corners of the world and liberates all human beings from human slavery across the whole globe. It clashes with all the forces of tyranny and establishes the system of the worship of Allah over the entire globe.

In the course of this movement, those who raise the movement carrying this religion do not stop after establishing government in any one region. They do not halt at any geographical, racial or national boundary. This movement changes the values of people. Within society the rank and position of people is determined anew. All values are built upon the standard of faith. People's introduction in society is on the basis of these new values, and the worth of every individual is determined anew. In an Islamic society the worth of individuals depends on how much struggle they have made for the establishment of religion, what trials have come upon them, and how they are in terms of piety, fear of God, morals and capability. These are the values which are determined in the form of events, and the Islamic movement expresses them, and the whole Islamic society and the Islamic movement is acquainted with such individuals. Therefore such individuals have no need at all to praise themselves or to demand any office or responsibility; firstly, they do not feel the need for it, and secondly, their purification and training have progressed to such an extent that they do not do such things.

Sometimes some people think that this was a characteristic of the earlier Islamic society, because history tells that the people of the first century were trained in the best manner. But they do not know that no such society can come into existence unless a movement of this kind is raised for it, and unless struggle is made for the establishment of an Islamic society by training people in the manner of the Companions of the Prophet. Whenever we establish such a society, we will have to pass through these very same paths. A movement will be raised; it will call people to embrace the religion of Islam anew, and in this way efforts will be made to bring people out of jahiliyyah. Then the people of jahiliyyah will persecute these workers in the same way. Some people will run away from the movement and take the path of apostasy, but some will remain firm on their path. For them, leaving the call and the movement will be like being thrown into fire. Then the conflict will be decided: Allah will grant victory to the movement, and an Islamic government will be established in some one place. From this centre the spread of the Islamic revolution will begin. At that time the mujahidin and the activists will have come fully to the fore. At that time the values and qualities of faith will have become clear, and no one will need to present an application for any office, because such people will be the features of society, and it will itself purify them and entrust them with some responsibility.

Sometimes the question is asked: after this initial stage, what will happen when the Islamic society is permanently established? This question is asked by those who do not know the reality of this religion. This religion always remains in the form of a movement; it never stops at any time. Its movement is for the purpose that all human beings should be freed from slavery to other human beings and be brought into the worship and servitude of Allah. This freedom and nearness should be attained by all the inhabitants of the entire globe, and people should worship Allah instead of the worship of tāghūt, and the movement should continue unceasingly, without boundaries of colour, race and geography.

When this movement continues without interruption, the steadfast, sincere and self-sacrificing people will stand out and rise to the top on their own. Because the movement continues, this society will never become stagnant, frozen and insipid, unless it deviates from the Islamic path. In short, the command to remain silent about one's own qualities, to purify the self, and not to be eager for position will remain in force, just as it came at the beginning within one circle. It will remain in force within that same circle and continue to function.

It may also be asked: when society expands and people do not even become acquainted with one another's abilities and personalities, then capable people will be compelled to advertise their abilities and to declare that they have such and such character and possess such and such capacities.

This question too is based on an illusion, and it rests on the practical situation of the present jahiliyyah. But this is not the situation of an Islamic society. In an Islamic society the people of a neighbourhood are acquainted with one another and at the same time are mutually considerate, because Islamic training, the formation of an Islamic society, its direction and its obligations necessarily require that its people become very well acquainted with one another. They recognize one another's abilities through the criteria of faith. Therefore it will not be a difficult matter in an Islamic society to select good people for the Majlis-e-Shura or for individual and collective services. As for the great offices, such as governor and ruler, the Imam himself can seek out people for them, those who are among the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd (the people who loosen and bind, i.e., the men of influence and decision). The members of the Imam's shura can also assist in this, and can help the amir and the Imam in finding good individuals. Then, as we have said, Islam is a movement, and jihad will continue until the Day of Resurrection. So when there is movement and jihad, how can any person of capacity remain hidden?

Those who think today about the Islamic system of life and its detailed organization, or who write on this subject, fall into a folly. These people want to enforce the codified jurisprudential principles of the Islamic system of life in a vacuum. Then they want the rulings that are actually established and dominant in this jahili society to be enforced. This jahili society has its own particular physiological structure, and this actually existing jahili society, from the Islamic point of view and from the point of view of the jurisprudential rulings of Islam, is a vacuum, and there is no possibility that the Islamic Shariah could be enforced within it, because the physiological structure of the present jahili society is one hundred percent opposed to the physiological structure of an Islamic society. As we have explained in detail, the physiological formation of an Islamic society consists of those personalities, those groups and those people who launched a movement for the Islamic system, struggled against jahiliyyah, and implemented the world of Islam in practical form; and they carried out practical struggle against jahiliyyah so that people might be brought out of jahiliyyah and entered into Islam. In this cause they bore all the pressures of jahiliyyah, endured every kind of violence and persecution from jahiliyyah, and in the all-encompassing war of jahiliyyah against the Islamic movement they remained the steadfast soldiers of Islam, and from beginning to end they took part in this struggle. As for the present jahili society, it is a stagnant society, established upon values that have no connection with Islam, nor does this society have any connection with the principles of faith. Therefore, from the standpoint of the Islamic Shariah, this society is a vacuum for Islam. And it is obvious that in such a vacuum the Islamic system cannot take root.

When researchers and writers of this kind begin to put Islamic injunctions into practical form, they are confronted at every step with perplexity and bewilderment. The first perplexity that seizes them is how to choose the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd or the Majlis-e-Shura. That is, how to devise a method by which people do not put themselves forward as candidates, do not praise themselves, and yet good people rise to the top. The difficulty such people face in this matter is that in the present societies in which we live, people are not even acquainted with one another. Moreover, in the present age such people are also rare who would meet the standards of capacity, chastity, trustworthiness and honesty. Likewise, these people are greatly perplexed about the method of selecting the Imam and the Caliph. Will the Caliph be chosen by the common people, or will the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd choose him? If the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd do not put themselves forward as candidates and do not purify themselves, and their selection is made by the Imam, then how will they choose the Imam? Will this not affect the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd? Then, if these people nominate the Imam, will they not be superior to the Imam, although the superior one is the Imam? And if the Imam selects or nominates the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd, then these people will not be pleasing to him, and in their selection the first consideration will not be that they are loyal to him... These and many other innumerable questions require answers, and because of the superficial thinking of these researchers they are not finding any answer.

I think such researchers have gone astray from this very point. The error of these people begins from the premise that they regard our present societies as Islamic societies, and they think that the principles and branches of the Islamic system will be enforced upon present jahili societies. They think that, given the physiological formation and moral values of present societies and communities, Islam will be enforced within them. Impossible, absurd and madness!

The folly and perplexity of these people begin from the premise that they regard the present jahili society also as an Islamic society, and their thinking is that Islamic injunctions and rules will be applicable in this society, and that the physiological structure and moral rulings and rules of this society will be applicable in this society, and the physiological structure and moral condition of this society will remain as they are.

This is the starting point of their bewilderment and perplexity, and when these people begin thinking and researching, we are in a vacuum, and in this vacuum these people go so far away and their orbit becomes so vast that they lose their own way.

The truth is that this jahili society in which we live is not an Islamic society. For this reason neither the Shariah can be enforced in it, nor can the jurisprudential constitution be enforced in it; and they cannot be enforced for the reason that the Islamic Shariah and the Islamic constitution are never enforced in a vacuum, because the Islamic system is a practical system and it can be enforced only in an Islamic society, not in a vacuum.

The physiological formation of an Islamic society is indeed different from the ideological formation of the present jahili society. The individuals and groups of an Islamic society are not those of the present society. Its individuals are entirely different and its groups are entirely other. The moral values of its individuals and groups come into existence during the movement, and they are very different and practical.

This is a modern and new society. It remains in constant motion. It is progressive, and its people, in comparison with the whole earth, are free people. They are not slaves of anyone on this earth, and from this society the forces of taghut disappear.

This problem and other problems of this kind, such as presenting oneself as qualified for a post, seeking a post, the selection of the Imam, the selection of the members of the shura and other such problems, people generally think about in a vacuum. These problems and their enforcement in jahili societies, this very way of thinking, is self-contradictory, especially when this jahili society is entirely contradictory to an Islamic society in its physiological structure. Its values, moral standards, concepts and thoughts are all the reverse of an Islamic society.

The modern banks and all their activities, insurance and its rules and regulations, the problems of birth control, and other such knots which these researchers try to untie, the correct solution regarding them cannot be presented within present society.

On these subjects, from the very beginning of the discussion, the researcher becomes a victim of perplexity, because his effort is to think about enforcing and putting into operation the rules and laws of the Islamic Shariah within the present jahili and filthy society, and this society is one hundred percent contradictory to Islamic injunctions. Therefore such researchers encounter difficulty in them. These people hope that by enforcing Islamic laws the jahili societies will become Islamic. The truth is that this is an extremely ridiculous thought.

The truth is that the Islamic society was not brought into existence by Islamic jurisprudence; rather, after the Islamic society came into existence as a result of the movement's struggle and the long conflict between the Islamic movement and jahiliyyah, and after the practical needs of an Islamic society came to the fore, Islamic jurisprudence, its rulings and its principles came into being. Therefore, in the modern age too, the existence of Islamic jurisprudence can come about only in this way: that an Islamic society is brought into existence through an Islamic revolution. The reverse of this is not possible.

Remember that the enforcement of Islamic jurisprudence and the Islamic Shariah is not possible in a vacuum, nor can any law remain established in a vacuum. The Islamic Shariah cannot be established in minds and books; it is a practical code of practical life, and that code is not of every practical life but of an Islamic life. Only in the atmosphere of an Islamic society can the Islamic system of life and Islamic law be enforced.

When the Islamic society comes into existence, and it comes into existence in the form of a movement, then at that time it will face the question whether it needs banks and commercial institutions or not. This question will arise at that time. Now, when the Islamic society does not even exist at all, how can we know in advance the needs of that society? Nor can we know anything about the shape of that society at that time or its size. How can we legislate for a society before its time? The Islamic Shariah's rules that are codified at present cannot be enforced in a jahili and unbelieving society at all, because the Islamic Shariah does not even acknowledge the existence of present jahili and unbelieving societies, and it has no interest in the problems of those jahili societies.

The calamity into which these researchers have fallen is that they regard present jahili societies as the reality and, considering Islam to be subordinate to them, they try to make it conform to them; but the actual situation is the reverse. The truth is that Islam is the reality, and it is our duty to keep making modern society subordinate to Islam. This work can be accomplished by only one means, namely, that a movement be raised for the establishment of an Islamic society in opposition to jahiliyyah. This movement should be for the establishment of the sovereignty of Allah on this earth. The system of Allah's sovereignty is precisely that in which people are subservient to none but Allah; they are not subject to any taghut, and in their lives only the Shariah reigns. Whenever anyone raises this movement, he will have to confront trials, tribulations and violence. When such a movement is subjected to violence, some people will bear these hardships, some will turn back on their heels, and some, confirming the message of Allah, will attain the station of martyrdom, while others will continue this struggle until Allah renders a correct decision between them and their people. When Allah decides between the revolutionaries and their peoples, they will be granted establishment in the land, and only then will the Islamic system of life be truly established. At that time all people will be imbued with Islam, and they will have attained an exalted station in this world by taking up Islamic values. At that time this society will have certain needs and requirements, and these needs and requirements will be entirely different from those of other jahili societies. The methods of fulfilling these needs and requirements will also be different. At that time the deduction of the injunctions of the Islamic system of life will be for an established society; an Islamic jurisprudence and Shariah will come into existence. This Shariah will not be in a vacuum, but this Shariah will be enforced in a defined and existing society, and the aims and needs of that society will also be defined.

Let someone tell us where is that society in this world in which the system of zakat is enforced, zakat is collected, it is spent on its true objects, and in whose every neighbourhood mutual love, mercy and a system of mutual support (takaful) exist; then the whole society has a system of social security (takaful), and the financial system of that society is not founded on extravagance, ostentation, self-display and hoarding of wealth. Its financial system is established on correct Islamic lines. Then, if such a system is established and such a society comes into existence, let it be demonstrated that in it insurance will be needed, and that those insurance rules will then conform to the circumstances, values and financial concepts of the Islamic society. If the Islamic society should need any insurance, let it be demonstrated that it must necessarily be exactly in the same form as the insurance system that exists in present jahili societies, which is based on jahili concepts and values and which has been brought into existence to meet the needs of the jahili society.

Then let it be demonstrated that a dynamic Islamic society will need restriction of progeny and birth control, just as the present non-Islamic society does.

When we cannot even determine the needs of an Islamic society under present conditions, nor do we have a definite picture of its size and shape, and this is not possible either, because the very physiological composition of an Islamic society is entirely different from the present jahili society. Its thinking, its values and its ... are also different. Therefore, those people who are now trying to codify laws for a society that does not exist at present, their effort will be unappreciated, because just as the Islamic society is currently in the air, so their endeavours too are in the air and fruitless.

As we have said again and again, the error in this matter begins here: these researchers consider present societies to be Islamic societies, and they want to extract rules from the pages of Islamic jurisprudence and impose them on these societies. They do not touch the constituent elements of present societies, and they leave the values, concepts and ... of these societies as they are.

Then, in the consciousness and subconsciousness of these gentlemen, there sits the notion that present jahili societies are the real and established reality, and that it is the duty of Islam to change itself and adapt to them. "They do not change themselves; they change the Qur'an..." Thus it becomes the duty of the religion of Islam to fulfil the demands of modern jahili society. Yet the demands of modern jahili society are entirely against Islam, and these demands want to expel a Muslim from Islam altogether.

My view is that the time has come for Islam to be exalted in the hearts and minds of the people of Islam. Now the people of Islam should abandon this approach, that Islam should keep going around fulfilling the demands of jahili society. The callers to Islam should now announce: O people! Become obedient servants of Islam, accept its commands with heart and soul; rather, O people! First of all, enter the religion of Islam. Declare that you are now only servants of Allah, and bear witness to La ilaha illa Allah, fulfilling all the requirements of the kalimah tayyibah, in the sense that there is no other sovereign on this earth besides Allah. He alone is Lord and Creator, Owner and Provider. The commands of Allah alone shall govern the lives of all people. Henceforth no human shall be the slave of another human, and no human shall make law for another human.

When people make this announcement, the sapling of the Islamic society will put forth shoots, and when a society comes into existence on the basis of this declaration, then Islamic jurisprudence will be implemented in it. At that time Islamic jurisprudence will fulfil all the needs of that society, and the Islamic Shari'ah will be enforced in practice.

As long as an Islamic society is not established as a result of an Islamic revolution, to rack one's brains over the constitutional and administrative injunctions of Islam is merely deceiving oneself. It is sowing seed in air and in a void, for no law ever grows in a void, just as no crop grows in the air.

٭٭٭

Working in the intellectual field of Islamic jurisprudence is an extremely interesting task, because in it there is no danger and no trial. But this is not an Islamic work, that is, it is not for Islam; nor is it in accordance with the temperament of this religion, nor is it the Islamic method of action. This method belongs only to those who, living a life of comfort and well-being, occupy themselves merely with scholarly and technical matters. But my view is that at this stage of the movement, to rack one's brains over the topics of Islamic jurisprudence is to waste one's life. In the present society, I think, there would be no enforcement of it in any case.

The religion of Islam does not perform the task of a lackey for jahiliyyah, nor does it accept becoming the obedient servant of jahiliyyah, whose mission is merely to keep providing justifications at all times for the desires of jahiliyyah. Whereas this jahili society is alienated from religion, distant from religion, and in a state of deficiency regarding religion, and while not obeying religion, this society seeks from religion a justification for its deeds.

It must be well understood that the jurisprudence of this religion and its injunctions neither develop in a void nor react in a void. An Islamic society, at the beginning, is one that accepts the sovereignty of Allah. It is this very society that in reality gives existence to jurisprudence, and it is this very society that develops it. It is not that some jurisprudential system gives existence to society.

The stages of the revival of Islam and its method of action have been one and the same from the beginning. The conversion of a society from jahiliyyah to Islam is certainly not an easy matter, and it does not happen by first moulding a pattern of jurisprudential injunctions, and people being trained in accordance with it, and that pattern having been prepared in advance in a void, so that when an Islamic society comes into being after the Islamic revolution, it is then enforced in it. The conversion of a society from jahiliyyah to Islam does not occur because of any legal system. Therefore people have the misconception that perhaps the Islamic society is not coming into existence because the legal system has not been prepared in detail. Some people are victims of this misconception in this matter, and some are victims of this misconception.

The truth is that an Islamic society is not coming into existence because certain tyrannical forces stand blocking its path. These tyrannical forces do not accept the principle of Allah's sovereignty. Because of this, in no Islamic country is a system based on Allah's lordship and sovereignty coming into existence. These tyrannical forces have in fact made people their own servants and slaves, and in this way these forces, and all the common masses under them, become afflicted with shirk. This is real shirk, and this shirk is connected with the particular prerogatives of Allah, Lord of the worlds.

On the basis of this doctrine, jahiliyyah establishes its own independent system on earth. It establishes this system also on the basis of these jahili concepts, and in it, alongside jahili concepts, it also relies on material forces.

The established system of this kind cannot be confronted with jurisprudential injunctions. Nor are jurisprudential injunctions equal in strength to this jahili system and its concepts. This jahiliyyah can be confronted only in this way: people are invited afresh to enter Islam, and then, with all forces together with Islamic concepts, jahiliyyah is confronted. In this arena, after the open struggle between Islam and jahiliyyah, whatever the outcome, it will come to light. Some people will become truly Muslim, and the rest of the nation will be opposed to them, and as a result of this struggle, Allah brings His decision between the Islamic movement and its people. When the Islamic movement, having become dominant, establishes an Islamic society, then the time comes for the codification of jurisprudential injunctions. The system and law that is established in this way is, in its true atmosphere, extremely natural, because it fulfils the needs of a living Islamic society. Legislation takes place for the real needs of this new society, and in it the size and shape of the law are natural. Now this society and its needs are not before us, and we cannot yet make any prediction about the society that will come into existence after the revolution. Nor can we determine its needs. Therefore, to occupy oneself now, before the time, with the work of codifying and arranging Islamic law, or to demand it, is contrary to the seriousness and sobriety of the religion of Islam.

The point I am making does not mean at all that the established explicit injunctions of the Qur'an and Sunnah are not legally enforceable at present. Rather, my purpose is that these injunctions were revealed for an Islamic society and are also to be enforced within an Islamic society. These injunctions are not enforced in practice at present. These injunctions can be enforced in practice only when an Islamic society is established, and the establishment of an Islamic society is an obligation on every Muslim who is currently living in a jahili society, so that the legal system of Islam may be enforced in it. Only those people can accomplish this task who rise up in the form of a movement carrying the religion, and who confront those tyrannical forces that have established this tyrannical system, and whose people, instead of obeying Allah alone, have become associators and are engaged in obeying those tyrannical forces.

When people grasp this point in the matter of the revival of religion, that when a jahili system is established it is necessary to set up an Islamic movement against it, then through this realisation the Islamic revolution begins, and then people rise up for the constructive struggle for the revival of Islam. The truth is that since human-made laws have taken the place of the Islamic law, the Islamic system has not remained, and this earth has become empty of real Islam. Although the call-houses remain, and the mosques remain, prayers are being offered and salah is being performed. This has been the situation for the last two hundred years. Among Muslims there is an emotional attachment to this religion, and this salah and this prayer create in them the comfort that Islam is well, although the tyrannical forces on this earth are bent on erasing its existence.

I say: Even before the Islamic acts of worship, the Islamic society had come into existence. Even before the mosques, the Islamic society had come into existence. This society and this community came into existence at the time when it was said to them: "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him." It should be remembered that these people who worshipped those idols did not keep their salah and their fasts, for salah and fasting were not obligatory at the time this verse was revealed. Worship of Allah alone meant this: regard Allah alone as your sovereign; and at that time there was no Islamic legal system either. And when people accepted Allah as their sovereign on this earth, then the Shari'ah came from the Sovereign. This Shari'ah also came in such a way that whenever this Islamic society was faced with a real need for a law, a law was revealed, or they themselves derived a law for themselves in the light of the Qur'an and Sunnah... This is the sole method of action, and this method will remain until the Day of Resurrection.

What could be an easier method of Islamic revolution than this: a caller gives a speech, explains the injunctions of Islam, and elucidates the Islamic law; people suddenly enter Islam, and the matter is finished. But this method is mere wishful thinking. It is a good desire. The reality is that the common people can enter the Islamic system, leaving tyrannical forces and jahiliyyah, only in accordance with this method, and that method is a lasting, gradual method of the call to Islam.

Its summary is this: an individual begins the call to Islam; a vanguard accepts his call. This vanguard confronts the existing system of jahiliyyah, and after that a conflict is set up between it and that jahili system. A war begins between these callers, who have risen from that same people, and the entire people, indeed the whole society. Allah gives victory to this vanguard, and people enter the religion of Islam in multitudes. And what is this religion of Islam? It is that system of Allah, other than which Allah does not tolerate any system.

"And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him" [Qur'an 3:85].

Perhaps this lengthy statement will make the position of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) clear: that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) was not in an Islamic society in which no one had any opportunity to seek office, and in which no one could demand any post. On the other hand, he was seeing that in this non-Islamic system he was being offered a position in which all powers were coming into his hands, and that he would be obeyed as ruler; thus he would get the opportunity to spread his beliefs throughout Egypt. Accordingly, in practice it happened that during his period of rule the doctrine of tawhid spread throughout Egypt. In that era, Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) so overshadowed Egyptian society that both the nobles of Egypt and the king of Egypt receded into the background.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 54–55 (part 1 of 3):

He said, "Make me in charge of the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I am a guardian who has knowledge." (12:55) Yusuf (peace be upon him) said, "Place the treasuries of the kingdom under my control. I am both a guardian and a knowledgeable person."

The summary of the coming task is that there are seven years of abundance, and in them there is a need to save a portion of the produce ..... , to run the affairs of the state in a good manner, to set right all the departments of the state, and to plan during the period of prosperity in such a way that it can be benefited from in times of hardship and drought. For this reason, Yusuf (peace be upon him) mentioned precisely those qualities that were necessary for such circumstances, namely ḥafīẓ and ʿalīm. This arrangement was beneficial for Egypt and all the surrounding regions and countries. Therefore he said, ﴿Indeed, I am a guardian who has knowledge﴾ (12:55). Yusuf's (peace be upon him) demand was not made so that he might take the ministry of finance and obtain some benefits for himself; rather, he was a man of sound judgment and an intellectual, and he considered that no one else was more suitable for this duty than himself. The coming period would be a period of famine, because the entire Egyptian nation and neighbouring peoples would face the great problem of arranging for grain and other provisions. In the seven good years there was the great task of economy, and in the seven difficult years there was the great task of maintaining supply. Yusuf (peace be upon him) did not ask for anything for his own person; rather, this was that great responsibility from which everyone was fleeing, and no one was ready to accept it gladly, considering it a windfall. Firstly, in the royal system there was the danger of being executed; secondly, it is not possible to control the common people in a state of hunger and destitution, because when the people are hungry they tear apart the officials like madmen. All these possibilities were before Yusuf (peace be upon him).

Here a doubt arises: that what Yusuf (peace be upon him) said and demanded, "Appoint me over the treasures of the earth, for I am a guardian and knowledgeable," is it not a demand for an office, which is severely disapproved of in the Islamic system? Since this is an explicit demand to be appointed to a post, and the hadith states: "By God, we do not entrust this matter to the one who asks for it" (agreed upon).

The second objection is that Yusuf (peace be upon him) himself here stated that he is a guardian and knowledgeable. This is in some sense a declaration of self-purification, and the Qur'an itself says: ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ ("Do not claim purity of your own selves"). The easy answer to this may be that these administrative principles were implemented in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, but it is not necessary that they were forbidden in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him) as well, because while there has been agreement among all the prophets on the principles of religion, administrative matters and legal rulings have differed from one to another.

But we do not give this as a superficial answer, because this matter needs to be examined with some depth, and its results are very profound and far-reaching. It has some further aspects and considerations, and it is necessary to view it from these angles in a broad perspective, so that in deriving the rulings of jurisprudence we may derive matters from this broad point of view and give a dynamic approach to the jurisprudential rulings as well. Because jurisprudential rulings, their methodology of derivation and the principles of jurisprudence have also become frozen during the period of stagnation and decline of the Muslims. They too need to be given a dynamic, movement-oriented approach.

The truth is that Islamic jurisprudence did not come into existence in a vacuum, nor can it be understood or implemented in a vacuum. The development of Islamic jurisprudence took place within a developing Islamic society. That society, in its developmental period, had to fulfil the needs of Islamic life. It was not Islamic jurisprudence that gave birth to an Islamic society; rather, within an Islamic society, Islamic jurisprudence developed to meet its needs. These are two great facts, and Islamic history bears witness to them. Unless we understand the relationship between the Islamic society and the formation of jurisprudence, we cannot understand Islamic jurisprudence, nor can we understand its dynamic and developmental status.

Those who today read these texts and take the codified rulings of jurisprudence, and who do not keep in view the fact that first an Islamic society came into existence and then jurisprudence came into existence, and who also do not look at the circumstances in which these texts were revealed, and how the Islamic jurisprudential issues were compiled, especially do not keep in view the environment, the society and the temperament in which these texts were revealed, such people want to implement this law in a vacuum, whereas no legal system is ever implemented in a vacuum; rather it is implemented in a society. Such people are in reality not jurists, nor are they experts in Islamic law. These people have in fact not understood the temperament of the Islamic system, nor the reality of this religion.

Dynamic jurisprudence is in fact different from the jurisprudence that exists in the pages of books, although dynamic jurisprudence too is based on the same principles and texts on which the jurisprudence of the pages is based. Dynamic jurisprudence also keeps in view the circumstances in which the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah were revealed. A practical jurist sees that the occasion of revelation and the circumstances of revelation cannot be separated from the original texts. If we consider a text in isolation from the circumstances in which it was revealed, our deduction and ijtihad will become wrong, and the jurisprudence formed in this way will not be correct.

This is why no divine jurisprudential command is such that it came on its own in a vacuum, without the influence of the environment and society in which it first appeared. No jurisprudential ruling or ijtihad has occurred in a vacuum, so it cannot remain in a vacuum.

Examples of the principle we have stated above are those rulings in which it is said that a person should not claim his own purity or should not present himself for an office. These rulings are derived from the verse ﴿So do not claim purity of your own selves﴾ and from the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "By God, we do not give this office to the one who asks for it."

These rulings came in a society which was an Islamic society, and in that Islamic society these rulings were in fact actually implemented. These rulings were meant for precisely such a society, so that they might fulfil the needs of an established Islamic society. The Islamic society of that time had its own historical background and its own particular organic structure; that society had its own specific and personal situation. These two rulings were such rulings as were to be implemented within a fully established Islamic society, and it was in precisely those circumstances that they were revealed. They were not revealed in a vacuum. Therefore we can implement these two rulings within an established Islamic society, a society whose composition, whose upbringing and whose organic movement is Islamic. Whenever such a society is established, such rulings and a system in accordance with them will be established within it. If there is no trace of an Islamic society anywhere, these rulings cannot be implemented in it, in a vacuum.

The same is the case with all Islamic rulings, but we do not think it appropriate here to give details about the other Islamic rulings.

The question is: why would people in an Islamic society not make themselves into a "Mithu" by praising themselves, and why would they not put themselves forward as candidates, and why would they not be able to campaign for their preferred individuals so that they may be selected for the Shura council, as governor, or for some other office?

The truth is that when an Islamic society is established, people will have no need for any propaganda to express their ability and merit. Moreover, in an Islamic society, office is a kind of responsibility, and only a fool would strive to take upon himself a responsibility without reason. The only exception is that one may desire such an office for the sake of seeking the pleasure of Allah, earning reward through serving humanity, or performing duties within society; but even then, it is only in the manner that someone places that office and responsibility upon him. Those who themselves make demands and run after offices are light-minded people, and their purpose in those offices is to obtain other objectives. Therefore it is necessary that such people are never offered these offices.

But this truth can be understood only when the establishment of an Islamic society and its temperament are understood, and its nature of formation is in mind. The truth is that movement and motion are the very life of any Islamic society. An Islamic society in fact comes into existence as a result of an Islamic movement. How? 

(1) For example, a message and a belief are sent down from Allah. A Messenger conveys it. In the time of prophethood, the Messenger himself used to convey it; after the period of prophethood, however, a caller in place of the Messenger calls to this same belief. Some people accept this call, whereas in the early days of the call the system of government is jahili, and this jahili system of government and this jahili society persecute the movement. In the period of trial, affliction and tribulation, some people abandon the movement and apostatise, while some stand firm and are martyred, and others wait and continue the work.

Those who bear difficulties and continue the work, Allah grants them victory. These people then become the instrument of the hand of power; Allah grants them establishment on earth, dominance and authority, because this is His permanent promise. In this way these people establish the rule of God on earth and implement the commands of Allah in it. This authority and establishment on earth is not for the sake of these people themselves; rather, this support and dominance is for the religion of Allah and to establish on earth the system of Allah's lordship.

This vanguard of the religion, carrying the religion, does not stop at any earthly boundary, nor does it confine itself within the bounds of any nation or lineage. It is not confined to any colour or lineage, nor to any language or form; these are very weak and unstable elements and limited circles. Rather, this vanguard, carrying this message, spreads throughout the corners of the world and liberates all human beings from human slavery across the whole globe. It clashes with all the forces of tyranny and establishes the system of the worship of Allah over the entire globe.

In the course of this movement, those who raise the movement carrying this religion do not stop after establishing government in any one region. They do not halt at any geographical, racial or national boundary. This movement changes the values of people. Within society the rank and position of people is determined anew. All values are built upon the standard of faith. People's introduction in society is on the basis of these new values, and the worth of every individual is determined anew. In an Islamic society the worth of individuals depends on how much struggle they have made for the establishment of religion, what trials have come upon them, and how they are in terms of piety, fear of God, morals and capability. These are the values which are determined in the form of events, and the Islamic movement expresses them, and the whole Islamic society and the Islamic movement is acquainted with such individuals. Therefore such individuals have no need at all to praise themselves or to demand any office or responsibility; firstly, they do not feel the need for it, and secondly, their purification and training have progressed to such an extent that they do not do such things.

Sometimes some people think that this was a characteristic of the earlier Islamic society, because history tells that the people of the first century were trained in the best manner. But they do not know that no such society can come into existence unless a movement of this kind is raised for it, and unless struggle is made for the establishment of an Islamic society by training people in the manner of the Companions of the Prophet. Whenever we establish such a society, we will have to pass through these very same paths. A movement will be raised; it will call people to embrace the religion of Islam anew, and in this way efforts will be made to bring people out of jahiliyyah. Then the people of jahiliyyah will persecute these workers in the same way. Some people will run away from the movement and take the path of apostasy, but some will remain firm on their path. For them, leaving the call and the movement will be like being thrown into fire. Then the conflict will be decided: Allah will grant victory to the movement, and an Islamic government will be established in some one place. From this centre the spread of the Islamic revolution will begin. At that time the mujahidin and the activists will have come fully to the fore. At that time the values and qualities of faith will have become clear, and no one will need to present an application for any office, because such people will be the features of society, and it will itself purify them and entrust them with some responsibility.

Sometimes the question is asked: after this initial stage, what will happen when the Islamic society is permanently established? This question is asked by those who do not know the reality of this religion. This religion always remains in the form of a movement; it never stops at any time. Its movement is for the purpose that all human beings should be freed from slavery to other human beings and be brought into the worship and servitude of Allah. This freedom and nearness should be attained by all the inhabitants of the entire globe, and people should worship Allah instead of the worship of tāghūt, and the movement should continue unceasingly, without boundaries of colour, race and geography.

When this movement continues without interruption, the steadfast, sincere and self-sacrificing people will stand out and rise to the top on their own. Because the movement continues, this society will never become stagnant, frozen and insipid, unless it deviates from the Islamic path. In short, the command to remain silent about one's own qualities, to purify the self, and not to be eager for position will remain in force, just as it came at the beginning within one circle. It will remain in force within that same circle and continue to function.

It may also be asked: when society expands and people do not even become acquainted with one another's abilities and personalities, then capable people will be compelled to advertise their abilities and to declare that they have such and such character and possess such and such capacities.

This question too is based on an illusion, and it rests on the practical situation of the present jahiliyyah. But this is not the situation of an Islamic society. In an Islamic society the people of a neighbourhood are acquainted with one another and at the same time are mutually considerate, because Islamic training, the formation of an Islamic society, its direction and its obligations necessarily require that its people become very well acquainted with one another. They recognize one another's abilities through the criteria of faith. Therefore it will not be a difficult matter in an Islamic society to select good people for the Majlis-e-Shura or for individual and collective services. As for the great offices, such as governor and ruler, the Imam himself can seek out people for them, those who are among the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd (the people who loosen and bind, i.e., the men of influence and decision). The members of the Imam's shura can also assist in this, and can help the amir and the Imam in finding good individuals. Then, as we have said, Islam is a movement, and jihad will continue until the Day of Resurrection. So when there is movement and jihad, how can any person of capacity remain hidden?

Those who think today about the Islamic system of life and its detailed organization, or who write on this subject, fall into a folly. These people want to enforce the codified jurisprudential principles of the Islamic system of life in a vacuum. Then they want the rulings that are actually established and dominant in this jahili society to be enforced. This jahili society has its own particular physiological structure, and this actually existing jahili society, from the Islamic point of view and from the point of view of the jurisprudential rulings of Islam, is a vacuum, and there is no possibility that the Islamic Shariah could be enforced within it, because the physiological structure of the present jahili society is one hundred percent opposed to the physiological structure of an Islamic society. As we have explained in detail, the physiological formation of an Islamic society consists of those personalities, those groups and those people who launched a movement for the Islamic system, struggled against jahiliyyah, and implemented the world of Islam in practical form; and they carried out practical struggle against jahiliyyah so that people might be brought out of jahiliyyah and entered into Islam. In this cause they bore all the pressures of jahiliyyah, endured every kind of violence and persecution from jahiliyyah, and in the all-encompassing war of jahiliyyah against the Islamic movement they remained the steadfast soldiers of Islam, and from beginning to end they took part in this struggle. As for the present jahili society, it is a stagnant society, established upon values that have no connection with Islam, nor does this society have any connection with the principles of faith. Therefore, from the standpoint of the Islamic Shariah, this society is a vacuum for Islam. And it is obvious that in such a vacuum the Islamic system cannot take root.

When researchers and writers of this kind begin to put Islamic injunctions into practical form, they are confronted at every step with perplexity and bewilderment. The first perplexity that seizes them is how to choose the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd or the Majlis-e-Shura. That is, how to devise a method by which people do not put themselves forward as candidates, do not praise themselves, and yet good people rise to the top. The difficulty such people face in this matter is that in the present societies in which we live, people are not even acquainted with one another. Moreover, in the present age such people are also rare who would meet the standards of capacity, chastity, trustworthiness and honesty. Likewise, these people are greatly perplexed about the method of selecting the Imam and the Caliph. Will the Caliph be chosen by the common people, or will the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd choose him? If the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd do not put themselves forward as candidates and do not purify themselves, and their selection is made by the Imam, then how will they choose the Imam? Will this not affect the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd? Then, if these people nominate the Imam, will they not be superior to the Imam, although the superior one is the Imam? And if the Imam selects or nominates the ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd, then these people will not be pleasing to him, and in their selection the first consideration will not be that they are loyal to him... These and many other innumerable questions require answers, and because of the superficial thinking of these researchers they are not finding any answer.

I think such researchers have gone astray from this very point. The error of these people begins from the premise that they regard our present societies as Islamic societies, and they think that the principles and branches of the Islamic system will be enforced upon present jahili societies. They think that, given the physiological formation and moral values of present societies and communities, Islam will be enforced within them. Impossible, absurd and madness!

The folly and perplexity of these people begin from the premise that they regard the present jahili society also as an Islamic society, and their thinking is that Islamic injunctions and rules will be applicable in this society, and that the physiological structure and moral rulings and rules of this society will be applicable in this society, and the physiological structure and moral condition of this society will remain as they are.

This is the starting point of their bewilderment and perplexity, and when these people begin thinking and researching, we are in a vacuum, and in this vacuum these people go so far away and their orbit becomes so vast that they lose their own way.

The truth is that this jahili society in which we live is not an Islamic society. For this reason neither the Shariah can be enforced in it, nor can the jurisprudential constitution be enforced in it; and they cannot be enforced for the reason that the Islamic Shariah and the Islamic constitution are never enforced in a vacuum, because the Islamic system is a practical system and it can be enforced only in an Islamic society, not in a vacuum.

The physiological formation of an Islamic society is indeed different from the ideological formation of the present jahili society. The individuals and groups of an Islamic society are not those of the present society. Its individuals are entirely different and its groups are entirely other. The moral values of its individuals and groups come into existence during the movement, and they are very different and practical.

This is a modern and new society. It remains in constant motion. It is progressive, and its people, in comparison with the whole earth, are free people. They are not slaves of anyone on this earth, and from this society the forces of taghut disappear.

This problem and other problems of this kind, such as presenting oneself as qualified for a post, seeking a post, the selection of the Imam, the selection of the members of the shura and other such problems, people generally think about in a vacuum. These problems and their enforcement in jahili societies, this very way of thinking, is self-contradictory, especially when this jahili society is entirely contradictory to an Islamic society in its physiological structure. Its values, moral standards, concepts and thoughts are all the reverse of an Islamic society.

The modern banks and all their activities, insurance and its rules and regulations, the problems of birth control, and other such knots which these researchers try to untie, the correct solution regarding them cannot be presented within present society.

On these subjects, from the very beginning of the discussion, the researcher becomes a victim of perplexity, because his effort is to think about enforcing and putting into operation the rules and laws of the Islamic Shariah within the present jahili and filthy society, and this society is one hundred percent contradictory to Islamic injunctions. Therefore such researchers encounter difficulty in them. These people hope that by enforcing Islamic laws the jahili societies will become Islamic. The truth is that this is an extremely ridiculous thought.

The truth is that the Islamic society was not brought into existence by Islamic jurisprudence; rather, after the Islamic society came into existence as a result of the movement's struggle and the long conflict between the Islamic movement and jahiliyyah, and after the practical needs of an Islamic society came to the fore, Islamic jurisprudence, its rulings and its principles came into being. Therefore, in the modern age too, the existence of Islamic jurisprudence can come about only in this way: that an Islamic society is brought into existence through an Islamic revolution. The reverse of this is not possible.

Remember that the enforcement of Islamic jurisprudence and the Islamic Shariah is not possible in a vacuum, nor can any law remain established in a vacuum. The Islamic Shariah cannot be established in minds and books; it is a practical code of practical life, and that code is not of every practical life but of an Islamic life. Only in the atmosphere of an Islamic society can the Islamic system of life and Islamic law be enforced.

When the Islamic society comes into existence, and it comes into existence in the form of a movement, then at that time it will face the question whether it needs banks and commercial institutions or not. This question will arise at that time. Now, when the Islamic society does not even exist at all, how can we know in advance the needs of that society? Nor can we know anything about the shape of that society at that time or its size. How can we legislate for a society before its time? The Islamic Shariah's rules that are codified at present cannot be enforced in a jahili and unbelieving society at all, because the Islamic Shariah does not even acknowledge the existence of present jahili and unbelieving societies, and it has no interest in the problems of those jahili societies.

The calamity into which these researchers have fallen is that they regard present jahili societies as the reality and, considering Islam to be subordinate to them, they try to make it conform to them; but the actual situation is the reverse. The truth is that Islam is the reality, and it is our duty to keep making modern society subordinate to Islam. This work can be accomplished by only one means, namely, that a movement be raised for the establishment of an Islamic society in opposition to jahiliyyah. This movement should be for the establishment of the sovereignty of Allah on this earth. The system of Allah's sovereignty is precisely that in which people are subservient to none but Allah; they are not subject to any taghut, and in their lives only the Shariah reigns. Whenever anyone raises this movement, he will have to confront trials, tribulations and violence. When such a movement is subjected to violence, some people will bear these hardships, some will turn back on their heels, and some, confirming the message of Allah, will attain the station of martyrdom, while others will continue this struggle until Allah renders a correct decision between them and their people. When Allah decides between the revolutionaries and their peoples, they will be granted establishment in the land, and only then will the Islamic system of life be truly established. At that time all people will be imbued with Islam, and they will have attained an exalted station in this world by taking up Islamic values. At that time this society will have certain needs and requirements, and these needs and requirements will be entirely different from those of other jahili societies. The methods of fulfilling these needs and requirements will also be different. At that time the deduction of the injunctions of the Islamic system of life will be for an established society; an Islamic jurisprudence and Shariah will come into existence. This Shariah will not be in a vacuum, but this Shariah will be enforced in a defined and existing society, and the aims and needs of that society will also be defined.

Let someone tell us where is that society in this world in which the system of zakat is enforced, zakat is collected, it is spent on its true objects, and in whose every neighbourhood mutual love, mercy and a system of mutual support (takaful) exist; then the whole society has a system of social security (takaful), and the financial system of that society is not founded on extravagance, ostentation, self-display and hoarding of wealth. Its financial system is established on correct Islamic lines. Then, if such a system is established and such a society comes into existence, let it be demonstrated that in it insurance will be needed, and that those insurance rules will then conform to the circumstances, values and financial concepts of the Islamic society. If the Islamic society should need any insurance, let it be demonstrated that it must necessarily be exactly in the same form as the insurance system that exists in present jahili societies, which is based on jahili concepts and values and which has been brought into existence to meet the needs of the jahili society.

Then let it be demonstrated that a dynamic Islamic society will need restriction of progeny and birth control, just as the present non-Islamic society does.
