When we cannot even determine the needs of an Islamic society under present conditions, nor do we have a definite picture of its size and shape, and this is not possible either, because the very physiological composition of an Islamic society is entirely different from the present jahili society. Its thinking, its values and its ... are also different. Therefore, those people who are now trying to codify laws for a society that does not exist at present, their effort will be unappreciated, because just as the Islamic society is currently in the air, so their endeavours too are in the air and fruitless.

As we have said again and again, the error in this matter begins here: these researchers consider present societies to be Islamic societies, and they want to extract rules from the pages of Islamic jurisprudence and impose them on these societies. They do not touch the constituent elements of present societies, and they leave the values, concepts and ... of these societies as they are.

Then, in the consciousness and subconsciousness of these gentlemen, there sits the notion that present jahili societies are the real and established reality, and that it is the duty of Islam to change itself and adapt to them. "They do not change themselves; they change the Qur'an..." Thus it becomes the duty of the religion of Islam to fulfil the demands of modern jahili society. Yet the demands of modern jahili society are entirely against Islam, and these demands want to expel a Muslim from Islam altogether.

My view is that the time has come for Islam to be exalted in the hearts and minds of the people of Islam. Now the people of Islam should abandon this approach, that Islam should keep going around fulfilling the demands of jahili society. The callers to Islam should now announce: O people! Become obedient servants of Islam, accept its commands with heart and soul; rather, O people! First of all, enter the religion of Islam. Declare that you are now only servants of Allah, and bear witness to La ilaha illa Allah, fulfilling all the requirements of the kalimah tayyibah, in the sense that there is no other sovereign on this earth besides Allah. He alone is Lord and Creator, Owner and Provider. The commands of Allah alone shall govern the lives of all people. Henceforth no human shall be the slave of another human, and no human shall make law for another human.

When people make this announcement, the sapling of the Islamic society will put forth shoots, and when a society comes into existence on the basis of this declaration, then Islamic jurisprudence will be implemented in it. At that time Islamic jurisprudence will fulfil all the needs of that society, and the Islamic Shari'ah will be enforced in practice.

As long as an Islamic society is not established as a result of an Islamic revolution, to rack one's brains over the constitutional and administrative injunctions of Islam is merely deceiving oneself. It is sowing seed in air and in a void, for no law ever grows in a void, just as no crop grows in the air.

٭٭٭

Working in the intellectual field of Islamic jurisprudence is an extremely interesting task, because in it there is no danger and no trial. But this is not an Islamic work, that is, it is not for Islam; nor is it in accordance with the temperament of this religion, nor is it the Islamic method of action. This method belongs only to those who, living a life of comfort and well-being, occupy themselves merely with scholarly and technical matters. But my view is that at this stage of the movement, to rack one's brains over the topics of Islamic jurisprudence is to waste one's life. In the present society, I think, there would be no enforcement of it in any case.

The religion of Islam does not perform the task of a lackey for jahiliyyah, nor does it accept becoming the obedient servant of jahiliyyah, whose mission is merely to keep providing justifications at all times for the desires of jahiliyyah. Whereas this jahili society is alienated from religion, distant from religion, and in a state of deficiency regarding religion, and while not obeying religion, this society seeks from religion a justification for its deeds.

It must be well understood that the jurisprudence of this religion and its injunctions neither develop in a void nor react in a void. An Islamic society, at the beginning, is one that accepts the sovereignty of Allah. It is this very society that in reality gives existence to jurisprudence, and it is this very society that develops it. It is not that some jurisprudential system gives existence to society.

The stages of the revival of Islam and its method of action have been one and the same from the beginning. The conversion of a society from jahiliyyah to Islam is certainly not an easy matter, and it does not happen by first moulding a pattern of jurisprudential injunctions, and people being trained in accordance with it, and that pattern having been prepared in advance in a void, so that when an Islamic society comes into being after the Islamic revolution, it is then enforced in it. The conversion of a society from jahiliyyah to Islam does not occur because of any legal system. Therefore people have the misconception that perhaps the Islamic society is not coming into existence because the legal system has not been prepared in detail. Some people are victims of this misconception in this matter, and some are victims of this misconception.

The truth is that an Islamic society is not coming into existence because certain tyrannical forces stand blocking its path. These tyrannical forces do not accept the principle of Allah's sovereignty. Because of this, in no Islamic country is a system based on Allah's lordship and sovereignty coming into existence. These tyrannical forces have in fact made people their own servants and slaves, and in this way these forces, and all the common masses under them, become afflicted with shirk. This is real shirk, and this shirk is connected with the particular prerogatives of Allah, Lord of the worlds.

On the basis of this doctrine, jahiliyyah establishes its own independent system on earth. It establishes this system also on the basis of these jahili concepts, and in it, alongside jahili concepts, it also relies on material forces.

The established system of this kind cannot be confronted with jurisprudential injunctions. Nor are jurisprudential injunctions equal in strength to this jahili system and its concepts. This jahiliyyah can be confronted only in this way: people are invited afresh to enter Islam, and then, with all forces together with Islamic concepts, jahiliyyah is confronted. In this arena, after the open struggle between Islam and jahiliyyah, whatever the outcome, it will come to light. Some people will become truly Muslim, and the rest of the nation will be opposed to them, and as a result of this struggle, Allah brings His decision between the Islamic movement and its people. When the Islamic movement, having become dominant, establishes an Islamic society, then the time comes for the codification of jurisprudential injunctions. The system and law that is established in this way is, in its true atmosphere, extremely natural, because it fulfils the needs of a living Islamic society. Legislation takes place for the real needs of this new society, and in it the size and shape of the law are natural. Now this society and its needs are not before us, and we cannot yet make any prediction about the society that will come into existence after the revolution. Nor can we determine its needs. Therefore, to occupy oneself now, before the time, with the work of codifying and arranging Islamic law, or to demand it, is contrary to the seriousness and sobriety of the religion of Islam.

The point I am making does not mean at all that the established explicit injunctions of the Qur'an and Sunnah are not legally enforceable at present. Rather, my purpose is that these injunctions were revealed for an Islamic society and are also to be enforced within an Islamic society. These injunctions are not enforced in practice at present. These injunctions can be enforced in practice only when an Islamic society is established, and the establishment of an Islamic society is an obligation on every Muslim who is currently living in a jahili society, so that the legal system of Islam may be enforced in it. Only those people can accomplish this task who rise up in the form of a movement carrying the religion, and who confront those tyrannical forces that have established this tyrannical system, and whose people, instead of obeying Allah alone, have become associators and are engaged in obeying those tyrannical forces.

When people grasp this point in the matter of the revival of religion, that when a jahili system is established it is necessary to set up an Islamic movement against it, then through this realisation the Islamic revolution begins, and then people rise up for the constructive struggle for the revival of Islam. The truth is that since human-made laws have taken the place of the Islamic law, the Islamic system has not remained, and this earth has become empty of real Islam. Although the call-houses remain, and the mosques remain, prayers are being offered and salah is being performed. This has been the situation for the last two hundred years. Among Muslims there is an emotional attachment to this religion, and this salah and this prayer create in them the comfort that Islam is well, although the tyrannical forces on this earth are bent on erasing its existence.

I say: Even before the Islamic acts of worship, the Islamic society had come into existence. Even before the mosques, the Islamic society had come into existence. This society and this community came into existence at the time when it was said to them: "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him." It should be remembered that these people who worshipped those idols did not keep their salah and their fasts, for salah and fasting were not obligatory at the time this verse was revealed. Worship of Allah alone meant this: regard Allah alone as your sovereign; and at that time there was no Islamic legal system either. And when people accepted Allah as their sovereign on this earth, then the Shari'ah came from the Sovereign. This Shari'ah also came in such a way that whenever this Islamic society was faced with a real need for a law, a law was revealed, or they themselves derived a law for themselves in the light of the Qur'an and Sunnah... This is the sole method of action, and this method will remain until the Day of Resurrection.

What could be an easier method of Islamic revolution than this: a caller gives a speech, explains the injunctions of Islam, and elucidates the Islamic law; people suddenly enter Islam, and the matter is finished. But this method is mere wishful thinking. It is a good desire. The reality is that the common people can enter the Islamic system, leaving tyrannical forces and jahiliyyah, only in accordance with this method, and that method is a lasting, gradual method of the call to Islam.

Its summary is this: an individual begins the call to Islam; a vanguard accepts his call. This vanguard confronts the existing system of jahiliyyah, and after that a conflict is set up between it and that jahili system. A war begins between these callers, who have risen from that same people, and the entire people, indeed the whole society. Allah gives victory to this vanguard, and people enter the religion of Islam in multitudes. And what is this religion of Islam? It is that system of Allah, other than which Allah does not tolerate any system.

"And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him" [Qur'an 3:85].

Perhaps this lengthy statement will make the position of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) clear: that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) was not in an Islamic society in which no one had any opportunity to seek office, and in which no one could demand any post. On the other hand, he was seeing that in this non-Islamic system he was being offered a position in which all powers were coming into his hands, and that he would be obeyed as ruler; thus he would get the opportunity to spread his beliefs throughout Egypt. Accordingly, in practice it happened that during his period of rule the doctrine of tawhid spread throughout Egypt. In that era, Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) so overshadowed Egyptian society that both the nobles of Egypt and the king of Egypt receded into the background.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 56:

Now we return within the context to the main theme and the story. Here the context does not say that Yusuf's (peace be upon him) request was accepted; rather, the request itself is the acceptance. The purpose of this is to show that, in the eyes of those people, Yusuf (peace be upon him) had now become a person of very great standing. Therefore, in place of a reply to the request, a comment is made on it, from which it is understood that Yusuf (peace be upon him) has also taken charge of his office. It is said:

﴿And thus did We establish Yusuf in the land, to take possession of it wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost. And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be God-fearing.﴾ (12: 56–57)

"Thus!" That is, by clearing him of the false accusation, by making the king of Egypt devoted to him, and then by placing him in the great office he had asked for, in this way We established a path to power for him. We strengthened his footing and he attained a lofty position in that land. That land, Egypt, was at that time a great and developed country, as if it were the whole country. ﴿To take possession of it wherever he willed﴾ (12: 56): wherever he wished to go, wherever he wished to stay, whatever post he wished to take. Look at this state in the light of the state in which they were in the dark well and every moment their lives were at stake, and then compare it with the state in which they were enduring the hardships of imprisonment.

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ (12: 56): We bring him out of difficulties into ease, and in exchange for hardships We give him joy; in exchange for fear We give him security, in exchange for imprisonment We give him freedom, and in exchange for lowliness in the eyes of people We give him a high station.

﴿And We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost﴾ (12: 56): Those who have firm faith in Allah, who place their trust in Him, who turn to Him, and who set right their conduct, their affairs and their relations with people in accordance with Him.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 57:**

ولا اجر الاخرة خير للذين امنوا وكانوا يتقون (12:57) "And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God." Therefore their basic reward will not be diminished, although the reward of the Hereafter is more precious than everything in this world, provided that a person sets out upon the path of faith and God-consciousness (taqwa) and makes his inner and outer life rest upon the path of God-consciousness.

Thus God removed the difficulties of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), gave him a high station in the land, and in the Hereafter gave him the glad tidings. This is the fitting reward of those who are patient and who do good.

٭٭٭

The wheel of time kept turning. Seven years of greenery and prosperity passed. The Qur'an has omitted the details of those seven years, so that what the people did in those years and what measures Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) adopted during them are not mentioned. How he ran the administration of the country was not described, since those affairs were bound to proceed in the best manner, because Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) had already said: ﴿Indeed, I am a guardian who is knowing﴾. The Qur'an also did not consider it necessary to mention the famine that came to the country, what befell the people in it, and how the drought came and how it went, because the interpretation of the dream of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) has, as it were, already told these details. He says:

ثم یاتی من بعد ذلک سبع ... مما تحصنون (12:48) ﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you have preserved.﴾

In the context of the narrative, neither the king nor any other royal official now appears on the scene. It is as though Yusuf (peace be upon him) alone is everything, bearing full responsibility on his shoulders in this frightful period. Now only Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) is on the stage, and he is in the glare of light from every direction. This is the reality that the story has also revealed through its artistic means.

As for the drought, the arrival of the brothers of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) shows that this drought had spread from the Sinai in that direction as far as Canaan, so these people reached Egypt in search of grain. In the region, it is the Egyptian government which, as a result of the measures of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), holds the responsibilities. The eyes of all neighbouring countries are upon Egypt; for all countries, Egypt has now become the granary. In such circumstances, in the story of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), his brothers now emerge, and in it, alongside the artistic features, religious purposes also come to the fore.

The famine and drought had engulfed the land of Canaan as well. Thus the brothers of Yusuf also set out for Egypt along with the other people, because Egypt had opened the stores of its grain to other countries. It had stored these reserves during the time of plenty. Now, before us the scene is this: these people are now guests of Hazrat Yusuf (peace be upon him), in circumstances where they do not know him, while he knows them well. For their inner selves have not changed much, whereas Hazrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) has changed. Then, in their thinking, it simply could not occur that Yusuf (peace be upon him) would be able to attain this position; that a Hebrew boy whom they had thrown into a dark well could reach here at all. And about twenty years had passed over him as well. Moreover, he is in the form of the ruler of Egypt, with his authority, his attendants, and the awe of his lofty office; how could this allow their imagination to turn in that direction?

Meanwhile, Hazrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) did not reveal his identity. He considered it appropriate that they be taught a little more of a lesson.

﴿وَجَاءَ إِخْوَةُ يُوسُفَ فَدَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ فَعَرَفَهُمْ وَهُمْ لَهُ مُنكِرُونَ﴾ (12:58)

"The brothers of Yusuf came and entered upon him. He recognised them, but they did not recognise him."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 59–61:

The context of the discourse shows that Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) seated them with honour and respect, and then began to instruct them in this manner.

﴿Wa lamma jahhazahum bijahazihim qal “’tuni bi-akhin lakum min abikum”﴾ (12:59): "When he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, 'Bring me your half-brother from your father.'" This shows that, already at the first meeting, they had become familiar with Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him). In this way they told the ʿAzīz of Egypt who they were, and that they had a half-brother whom our father does not wish to separate from himself, which is why he did not come. When their goods were ready, Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) said that he wished to meet this brother of theirs. "Do you not see that I give full measure to buyers, and that if your brother comes, I will also pay his share, and I will honour you as I honour the others?"

﴿Alā tarawna annī ūfil-kayla wa anā khayrul-munzilīn. Fa-in lam tatūnī bihī falā kayla lakum ʿindī wa lā taqrabūn﴾ (12:59–60): "Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts? But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no grain for you with me, and you shall not even come near me."

They knew that after the disappearance of Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him), Hadrat Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) kept Yusuf's brother with him at all times. Therefore they said that bringing him would not be an easy task for them, since their father would not be ready to let him go. In any case, they would try to bring him with them on another occasion.

﴿Qālū sanurāwidu ʿanhu abāhu wa innā lafāʿilūn﴾ (12:61): "They said, 'We will strive to persuade our father to send him, and we will certainly do so.'" The word "nurāwidu" shows that they understood that this task would require great effort on their part.

Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) ordered his servants to return to them, in their baggage, the money or goods they had brought in exchange for grain. It is possible that this contained some cash, or some rare desert produce, or leather and other items such as wool, which sell at a good price in cities. The purpose was that when they opened their loads, they would be astonished to see their own goods and would recognise that these were indeed their possessions.

They knew that after the disappearance of Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him), Hadrat Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) kept Yusuf's brother with him at all times. Therefore they said that bringing him would not be an easy task for them, since their father would not be ready to let him go. In any case, they would try to bring him with them on another occasion.

﴿Qālū sanurāwidu ʿanhu abāhu wa innā lafāʿilūn﴾ (12:61): "They said, 'We will strive to persuade our father to send him, and we will certainly do so.'" The word "nurāwidu" shows that they understood that this task would require great effort on their part.

Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) ordered his servants to return to them, in their baggage, the money or goods they had brought in exchange for grain. It is possible that this contained some cash, or some rare desert produce, or leather and other items such as wool, which sell at a good price in cities. The purpose was that when they opened their loads, they would be astonished to see their own goods and would recognise that these were indeed their possessions.

Qur'anic verse: And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, that they may come back."

Translation of the Urdu passage:

Yusuf (peace be upon him) signaled to his servants: "Secretly put back into their baggage the goods which these people paid in exchange for the grain." Yusuf (peace be upon him) did this in the hope that when they reached home and found their returned property, they would recognize it (or would be grateful for that generosity), and it is not unlikely that they would then come back.

Now Yusuf (peace be upon him) remains in Egypt, and in Kan'an Ya'qub (peace be upon him) and the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) are on the scene. The Qur'an is silent about their return.

Verses 63 to 66

It appears that these people went straight to their father's presence to greet him. Before even opening their goods, they considered it necessary to tell their father that a decision had been made about them: unless we bring our younger brother before the Aziz of Egypt, no further grain will be given to us. Thus, upon arriving, they immediately began to press their father to send the younger brother with them, so that they might obtain an extra camel-load of grain, and they undertook to take responsibility for his protection.

﴿Then when they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, we have been denied further measure of grain, so send our brother with us that we may obtain measure, and we will surely be its guardians."﴾ (12:63) Now the hidden apprehensions of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) come to the surface. They had made a similar firm pledge concerning Yusuf (peace be upon him) as well. Thus he expresses his grief.

He said, "Shall I entrust him to you as I entrusted his brother to you before? Nay, Allah is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."

Verse 64 continues: "[Jacob] said: 'Shall I entrust him to you as I entrusted his brother to you before?' [He said:] 'Leave that. Keep your false promises to yourselves and guard yourselves. I seek the protection of Allah and the mercy of Allah. He alone is the Guardian.'"

﴿فَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ حَافِظًا وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ﴾ "So Allah is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful." When they had settled their animals and rested from the journey, and they opened their baggage to dispose of the grain they had brought, they found that all the goods they had paid to buy grain had been returned to them, and their own property had been given back along with their grain.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) had placed their goods back in their saddlebags along with the grain. So when they opened their bags, they found their property. Therefore they said: "O our father, we have been denied further measure of grain, and this was done so that they would be compelled to take our brother with us." Yusuf (peace be upon him) wished to teach them a lesson, and this was one part of it. They presented the return of their goods as evidence that their demand to take their brother with them was not an act of injustice or oppression.

When they opened their belongings, they found that their merchandise had been returned to them as well. Seeing this, they exclaimed: "O our father, what more could we want? Look, our merchandise has also been returned to us. Now we will go back and bring provisions for our families, we will protect our brother, and we will bring an extra camel-load as well. That much grain will be easily obtained."

The gist of their argument is that they seek only the good of their family. Since they are going in search of provisions for the family, it is evident that they will protect their brother. Because of their brother, they will obtain an extra camel-load of grain. When the brother is with them, his share of the provisions will certainly be given.

From their statement that "we will bring an extra camel-load of grain," it appears that Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) used to give each person one camel-load of grain. No one was permitted to take as much grain as they wished, because during the period of drought it was wise to control distribution so that everyone would continue to receive a little grain.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 66:

Yaqub (peace be upon him) reluctantly accepted their demand, but set one condition, and a very strict one.

Qala lan ursilahu ... yuhat bikum (12:66). Their father said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in Allah's name that you will certainly bring him back to me, unless you are completely encompassed (by some calamity)."

That is, you must swear by Allah that you will bring him back, unless you are all surrounded and there is no means left for you to escape, and circumstances render you helpless.

Falamma atawhu mawthiqahum ... wakil (12:66). "When they gave him their solemn pledge, he said, 'Allah is the Guardian over what we have said.'" That is, for the sake of emphasis, to make the matter firm, and for further admonition and fear of Allah, he made Allah a witness. After this further emphasis, Yaqub (peace be upon him) now gives them further advice: take precautionary measures when entering the kingdom of Egypt.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 67:

Verse 67

Hazrat Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said: ﴿The command belongs only to Allah﴾. This statement requires deep reflection. From its context it becomes clear that Allah's decreed and compulsory commands run through this universe in such a way that no separation from them is possible within it. There is no deviation (takhalluf) from them, and there is no escape from these commands. This is precisely the meaning of the words in the Articles of Faith: "I believe in Allah... and in the Divine Decree, its good and its evil, is from Allah, the Exalted."

Allah's creative (takwini) and decreed (taqdiri) commands are enforced upon people in this world, and their implementation does not depend upon the will and choice of people. Alongside these compulsory and decreed Divine commands, there are also Divine commands that fall within the sphere of human choice. These are the legal (shar'i) commands, which the Qur'an and the Sunnah issue as commands and prohibitions. The ruling on these commands is similar to that of the decreed and creative commands. The only difference is that in legal commands people are free to implement them or not, and upon this their deeds in worldly life and the hereafter bring about results and rulings, and reward and punishment are decided. However, people cannot become Muslims until they also implement Allah's legal commands in their entire lives.

Now the caravan moves on, and they act upon their father's counsel.

Verse 68

Translation: The question here is why Prophet Ya'qub (peace be upon him) gave them this counsel. Why, on this occasion, does their father say that they should not enter through one gate but through separate gates?

The narrations and the tafsir works have said things far-fetched on this matter, though there was no need for them at all. Some commentators have even written things that go against the context of the Qur'an. Had the Qur'an wished to state a cause for this, it would certainly have mentioned it, but the Noble Qur'an has said only this much:

﴿And Ya'qub had a need in his soul, which he fulfilled﴾ (12:68). "There was a disquiet in the heart of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and he made his own effort to remove it." Therefore, the commentators should have restricted themselves to what the Qur'an has said, and confined their opinions to the atmosphere and setting in which this counsel was given and in which this matter was taking place. In that setting, Prophet Ya'qub (peace be upon him) harboured anxieties about the safety of his sons, and he thought that if they entered through separate gates without drawing attention, the danger he feared might perhaps be averted. But along with this, he also said that he could not protect them from Allah's decree: judgment belongs to none but Allah, and trust should be placed in Him alone. Nevertheless, there was a disquiet in his heart, and his intuition sensed some danger, and he addressed it through this counsel. Yet he knew that Allah's will would be carried out, and this knowledge had been conveyed to him by Allah and was part of his prophetic knowledge.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ (12:68). "But most people do not understand the reality of the matter." Now, what was the real cause? It is possible that he wished to protect them from the evil eye of envious people, or it could be that if they went as a group, the kingdom of Egypt might make it a matter of security for itself, or that they might be moved to jealousy by its splendour and grandeur on entering, or that they might be taken for thieves. Whatever the case, clarifying or specifying it here makes no difference. Yes, a reader and commentator would indeed suffer the loss that he would speak at length on these causes, straying from the real Qur'anic theme and purpose, and a chain of "it is said" would begin. Discussions of this kind, filled with hearsay, often take the discussion far away from the purely Qur'anic atmosphere and subject.

This is Sayyid Qutb's commentary (Fi Zilal al-Quran) on Surah Yusuf (12), verse 69, translated from the Urdu.

It is appropriate that we record this counsel and this journey in the same manner in which the Holy Qur'an has taken them. Now, with the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), we meet them in the next scene as follows:

Verse No. 69

In this scene we see that the meeting of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his full brother is arranged quickly. Then Yusuf (peace be upon him), without any preamble, informs his brother that he is his brother Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he also gives him the advice that he should forget the treatment that the other brothers had meted out to them before. Distressing memories of the past are, in any case, a part of a person's life, and since he had lived in Kan'an within the same family in which these events had taken place, these were necessarily distressing and painful for him at all times.

Why did the context mention this matter first? Whereas the natural course is that this conversation between the brothers probably did not take place at the very moment when this delegation met Yusuf (peace be upon him), the ruler of Egypt, but rather it took place when Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his [so-called] "false" brother were alone. Yes, when these people met Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he saw his brother after the long separation, the thought would have come to his heart first that he should inform the brother of this.

Since this was the first thought, in this scene it is presented in the form of the thought of Yusuf (peace be upon him). This is a very subtle and beautiful style of expression of the Qur'an, and only those people who know the technical subtleties of speech can truly enjoy it.

In this scene too, certain events are cut out as being unnecessary to narrate. For example, the hospitality of the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and the conversation that took place among them during it, and the scene of the departure of the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), are omitted. In this scene we see that Yusuf (peace be upon him) takes a particular measure to keep his brother with him, so that his brothers may be taught a lesson, indeed many lessons, which were necessary for them, and so that people who come until the Day of Resurrection may also take admonition from it. Accordingly, this measure is made a part of the everlasting Book.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 70–78:

This is an extremely interesting scene. It contains varied movements, expressions and surprises, much like a highly effective, emotional and vivid dramatic scene. But the mastery lies in the fact that the Holy Qur'an narrates living and real events in a most effective manner.

The movement behind the scene is this: Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) is having the king's goblet or cup placed in the baggage of his brother. It is said that this cup was used both for drinking and as a measure for grain. In that era, measuring wheat with a golden measure is not a surprising matter, because during this period of famine wheat was more valuable than gold. Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him), working behind the scenes, is having this cup placed in the baggage of his brother so that, in accordance with the instructions of Allah, this plan may be used to detain his brother. The details are yet to come.

Now, when this caravan has been loaded and has set out to return to Canaan, a herald appears and calls out in the form of a public proclamation, and this announcement is for the entire caravan.

﴿Ayyatuha al-'ir innakum lasariqun﴾ (12:70) "O caravan! Surely you are thieves." The brothers of Yusuf tremble with fear, because the accusation of theft has fallen upon the entire caravan. Its significance for them is greater still, because they are the sons of Prophet Ya'qub (peace be upon him), son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim (peace be upon them all). These people take back their animals and baggage so that an investigation into this accusation can be carried out.

"They turned back to them and said, 'What is it that you are missing?'" (12:71)

So the attendants, whose duty it was to prepare their loads, and the guards, among whom was this announcer, said to them:

"They said, 'We are missing the king's measuring cup.'" — "The king's officials said, 'We cannot find the king's goblet'" [note: translating as stands] 

Let me be precise and provide the full translation of the passage:

The king's officials said, "We have lost the king's goblet." [The Qur'anic text: ﴿قَالُوا نَفْقِدُ صُوَاعَ الْمَلِكِ﴾ (12:72) "They said, 'We are missing the king's goblet.'"] At this point, another person comes onto the scene and announces a reward, a large sum of reward, that if anyone returns it voluntarily, this valuable reward will be given. ﴿وَلِمَن جَاءَ بِهِ حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ وَأَنَا بِهِ زَعِيمٌ﴾ (12:72) "Whoever brings it will receive a camel-load [of grain], and I am its guarantor." Za'im (زعیم) in the sense of ḍāmin (guarantor): that I will give him a camel-load of grain.

But these gentlemen were fully certain that they were innocent, since they had done no wrong. Nor had they come in order to commit such acts as would destroy mutual trust and damage the international relations of different countries. Therefore they give an oath-bound statement:

﴿قَالُوا تَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ عَلِمْتُم مَّا جِئْنَا لِنُفْسِدَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ (12:73) "They said, 'By Allah, you know well that we did not come to make mischief in the land.'" The brothers said, "By God, you know well that we have not come to this country to cause corruption." You also know our history, our lineage and our standing, and our outward position is also visible.

﴿وَمَا كُنَّا سَارِقِينَ﴾ (12:73) "And we were never thieves." Such a wicked act could never proceed from us, never at all. The king's agents and guards said.

"They said, 'We are missing the king's measuring cup.'" — "The king's officials said, 'We cannot find the king's goblet'" [note: translating as stands] 

Let me be precise and provide the full translation of the passage:

The king's officials said, "We have lost the king's goblet." [The Qur'anic text: ﴿قَالُوا نَفْقِدُ صُوَاعَ الْمَلِكِ﴾ (12:72) "They said, 'We are missing the king's goblet.'"] At this point, another person comes onto the scene and announces a reward, a large sum of reward, that if anyone returns it voluntarily, this valuable reward will be given. ﴿وَلِمَن جَاءَ بِهِ حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ وَأَنَا بِهِ زَعِيمٌ﴾ (12:72) "Whoever brings it will receive a camel-load [of grain], and I am its guarantor." Za'im (زعیم) in the sense of ḍāmin (guarantor): that I will give him a camel-load of grain.

But these gentlemen were fully certain that they were innocent, since they had done no wrong. Nor had they come in order to commit such acts as would destroy mutual trust and damage the international relations of different countries. Therefore they give an oath-bound statement:

﴿قَالُوا تَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ عَلِمْتُم مَّا جِئْنَا لِنُفْسِدَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ (12:73) "They said, 'By Allah, you know well that we did not come to make mischief in the land.'" The brothers said, "By God, you know well that we have not come to this country to cause corruption." You also know our history, our lineage and our standing, and our outward position is also visible.

﴿وَمَا كُنَّا سَارِقِينَ﴾ (12:73) "And we were never thieves." Such a wicked act could never proceed from us, never at all. The king's agents and guards said.

"They said, 'Then what shall be its penalty, if you are lying?'" This question reveals the wisdom that Allah taught Yusuf (peace be upon him) through this plan. In the law of Yaqub (peace be upon him), the rule was that a thief would be taken as a bondsman or slave in exchange for the stolen property and the crime. Since the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) were fully certain of their own innocence, they gladly agreed that the matter be decided according to the law of Yaqub, whoever the guilty party might be. Thus the scheme that Allah devised for Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother reached its fulfillment.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 75:

"They said: 'Its requital—he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself shall be its requital. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers.'" They said: "Its penalty? The one in whose baggage it is found, he himself shall be its recompense. This is how we punish wrongdoers."

All this conversation was taking place in the presence of Hazrat Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he was seeing and hearing all of it. This is because he himself ordered the search, and his wisdom made him understand that the bags of the other brothers should be searched first, so that there would be no suspicion about the investigation and the plan.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 12, verse 76:

﴿So he began with their bags, before the bag of his brother.﴾ (12:76) "Then Yusuf (peace be upon him) began searching their bags before his brother's, and then he brought out the missing item from his brother's bag."

At this point the Qur'an does not describe the terror and distress into which the brothers of Yusuf suddenly fell. They were fully certain that they were innocent. They had even given a sworn statement, and they had given it in one voice. The Qur'an left this part of the scene to human imagination, because on such occasions such impressions appear on their own. This impression was left to the human imagination and a comment was made on the event, so that a reader might step a little outside the terror and shame in which the sons of Yaqub were caught.

﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾ (12:76) "In this way We planned for Yusuf (peace be upon him), a plan that was extremely profound."

﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ (12:76) "He had no right to hold his brother under the king's religion (law)." That is, if the case had been decided according to the royal law, Yusuf (peace be upon him) could not have detained his brother on his own authority; he could only have punished him as a thief. But the brothers proposed that the thief should be judged according to their own religion. This is the plan whose causes Allah taught to Yusuf (peace be upon him). This is the plan devised by Allah on Yusuf's behalf.

The word "kayd" in Arabic refers to a secret plan, and in lexical usage it is used in both good and bad senses. However, it has commonly come to be used more in the bad sense. Apparently, here the event is also outwardly an evil for his brothers, since it became difficult for them to face their father. Then for Yaqub (peace be upon him) too it is a painful matter for the time being. Therefore the Qur'an, keeping in view the outward aspect of the event, used the word "kayd" for it, which is a very subtle style of expression in the Qur'an.

﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless Allah willed it﴾ (12:76) "In the king's law he could not seize his brother, unless Allah willed it, as Allah devised this plan for them."

This final comment also makes clear that Allah had granted Yusuf (peace be upon him) very great elevations and very great knowledge.

﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ (12:76) "We raise the ranks of whomever We wish." But at the same time a warning is also given that the knowledge of Allah is the highest and the most exalted.

﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is One who is All-Knowing﴾ (12:76) "And above every person of knowledge is one who knows more." This is a subtle caution.

Here the Qur'an, in this verse, "Thus did We plan for Yusuf... he could not detain his brother under the king's religion," uses the word "din" in a specific sense, and this is a very technical and terminological usage: meaning system and law, because in the legal system of Egypt the penalty for a thief was not that he be kept in exchange for the crime. This penalty existed only in the legal system of Yaqub (peace be upon him). The brothers of Yusuf had agreed that the case be decided according to their law. When the cup was found in his brother's bag, Yusuf (peace be upon him) enforced their own law upon them. Here the Qur'an applies "al-din" to system and law.

This is a very clear and explicit meaning of din, and in the jahiliyyah of the twentieth century this meaning has disappeared from everyone's mind: from the minds of those who call themselves Muslims, and from the minds of those who are the propagators and followers of this jahiliyyah.

These people have confined the meaning of din to worship and religious rites. They think that whoever believes in the oneness of Allah, considers the Messenger truthful, believes in the angels and the books, accepts all the messengers, believes in the Hereafter, and holds that good and bad fate are from Allah, and then acts upon the obligations and acts of worship, is simply a firm religious person. Even though in other matters of life he obeys other lords and other rulers, and makes decisions according to the laws and shari'ah of others, whereas this verse clearly states that system, law and shari'ah are a matter of din, and the meaning of the din of Allah is Allah's complete system of life.

The meaning of "al-din" has been so restricted and narrowed that it has become confined to worship and beliefs alone. But the din presented by all the prophets, from Adam (peace be upon him) to Muhammad (ﷺ), did not have such a restricted meaning.

The meaning of din has always been that complete servitude be rendered to Allah. Those matters that are part of the shari'ah should be acted upon, and all matters that are contrary to the shari'ah should be abandoned. Just as Allah alone is the ruler of the heavens, so too on earth the sovereignty of Allah alone should be established, and Allah alone should be regarded as the Lord of all humans, that is, He alone should be the ruler, He alone the lawgiver, and His commands and prohibitions alone should prevail. The important question is: who are those in the din of Allah, and who are those in the din of the king? In this sense, those who obey the system and law of Allah are in the din of God, and those who accept the system and law of the king are in the din of the king. If these people commit shirk, then they commit shirk in beliefs and ideas, and they also commit shirk in system, law and constitution.

These are the logical and self-evident consequences of the meaning of din, and they are among the self-evident principles of the Islamic worldview.

Nowadays some sympathisers of the common people put forward the excuse that these people do not understand the meaning of "din Allah", and therefore such people neither demand that Islamic law and constitution be enforced, nor strive for it. Will the ignorance of these people and their lack of knowledge of the true meaning of din then become a ground for their excuse?

I do not think that not knowing the meaning of din and being unaware of its reality makes anyone religious. Conviction in a reality arises only when a person knows that reality. If people have no knowledge of a belief, how can they become adherents of it, and how can they be called people of that belief when they do not even understand its meaning?

It may be that ignorance of the reality of din will be a cause of some leniency in their reckoning in the Hereafter, or a reduction in punishment, and that the reckoning will be taken from those who did not teach them din, although they were acquainted with its true meaning. But this is a matter connected with the otherworldly reckoning, and the question of the punishment of all people of jahiliyyah to whom the call has not reached. Debating it is not very beneficial for us, nor is it our concern. Our duty is to call all people to Islam and to reach each and every one of them. Along with this, our duty is also to explain to people the reality of their present din: that this din is definitely not the din of Allah. The din of Allah is that which exists in the form of its texts as a system of life and a system of law. Thus whoever, together with Islamic beliefs, also establishes and enforces Allah's system and law will be in the religion of Islam. Whoever establishes the system of some king or other person will be in that system and din. This matter is not disputed.

Those who are unacquainted with the very meaning of this din, there is no possibility that they hold this din as a belief, because their ignorance is connected to the foundation of din, and one who has no knowledge of the reality of a thing is, both rationally and in fact, no longer able to hold belief in that thing, since belief comes after knowledge. It is established by clear guidance that belief is not possible without knowledge.

Therefore it is better for us to present to people the true meaning of din and the reality of din, instead of making unwarranted excuses for them, seeking pretexts for them, and becoming more compassionate toward them than Allah the Generous, while in reality they are not within the din of Allah. The policy regarding such people should be that they be told plainly what their position is, whether they adopt the din or abandon it.

This policy is beneficial for us and also beneficial for these common people. In this way we will also be spared from bearing the consequences of the misguidance of these ignorant ones, because these people, not having grasped the meaning of din, have not remained adherents of din at all. If we present the true reality of din before those who in fact are not within the religion of Islam but within the religion of the king and others, it is possible that their conscience will awaken and they will in reality enter the religion of Islam.

This has been the policy of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this should be the policy of all callers to the truth, in every time and place, against all the ignorant and the worshippers of jahiliyyah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 77–78:

After this brief and instructive remark, let us now return to the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him). Circumstances have brought them to this difficult stage, and the hidden enmity, hatred and envy they harboured against Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother have now come to the surface. Thus, to absolve themselves of this accusation, they place the blame on the children of Yaqub's (peace be upon him) other wife.

﴿Qalu in yasriq faqad saraqa akhun lahu min qabl﴾ (12:77). The brothers said: "If he steals, it is nothing strange; his brother (Yusuf, peace be upon him) also stole before him."

In the store of our tafsir literature, lengthy commentaries, narratives and reports have been related on this accusation, all of which are based on Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin). The point is that theft from him is not surprising, because his brother (Yusuf, peace be upon him) had already committed this crime before. In other words, they had not told a lie to their father about Yusuf (peace be upon him). Now, are they not telling a lie before the Aziz of Egypt, so that they may free themselves from this disgrace and thereby separate themselves somewhat from Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother? In this way they reveal their old hatred and envy towards Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother. The truth is that they made this completely baseless and false accusation against Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him).

﴿Fa-asarraha Yusufu fi nafsihi wa lam yubdihā lahum﴾ (12:77): "Yusuf (peace be upon him) kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them." In response to this accusation, Yusuf (peace be upon him) did not disclose his true situation to them; he swallowed the matter and did not show his feelings. Although he knew that he and his brother were innocent, he said only this:

﴿Qala antum sharrun makanan﴾ (12:77): "You are very evil in position." That is: you are making this false accusation, and in comparison to the one you are accusing, you yourselves are very wicked.

﴿Qala antum sharrun makanan﴾ (12:77): "Yusuf (peace be upon him) said, you are very wicked." That is: in comparison to the one on whom you are levelling the charge of theft, you yourselves are very wicked in the sight of Allah. What Yusuf (peace be upon him) said was not mere abuse but the truth.

﴿Wallahu a'lamu bima tasifun﴾ (12:77): "Allah knows best what you allege." He knows the reality of this incident and also the reality of your accusation. Lesson No. 110: Explanation of the Verses

Verses 80 to 101

The brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), having now despaired of getting back their younger brother, hold a consultative assembly away from the court of Yusuf (peace be upon him). This too is a strange scene. The context does not mention the views and proposals of everyone; rather, only the final statement and the decisive proposal of this consultation are given here.

Verses 80 to 82

Among the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), the eldest brother first reminds them that their father has taken a firm covenant from them, and that earlier you had also wronged Yusuf (peace be upon him). He acknowledges this. Then he gives the decisive proposal: that they will not leave Egypt until their father gives permission or Allah decides something, and that they are bound by Allah's decision in any case. What should they do? So he said to them: go and tell your father plainly that your son has committed theft. He was caught; this is what we know and what we have witnessed. If he is innocent and the real truth is something else, then he is unaware of it. They never expected that such an incident would befall them. This is the outward aspect of the matter. If the real matter is something else, then it is an unseen matter, and we do not know it; we are not charged with knowing it, and this matter was unseen to them, and no one can defend an unseen event. And if you do not believe our word, you may ask the people of the city, and you may also ask the caravan with which we came from Egypt, for they were not alone; caravans are constantly going to Egypt these days, and people come from there bringing grain. All the regions around Egypt are in the grip of famine; there is severe drought.

٭٭٭

Now, in what state they returned, and how their journey went, these details have been omitted here. These people now stand before their grieving father. They relayed the account. Only a brief reply from the grieving father is quoted in the context, in extremely sorrowful words. But in his words there still remains a ray of hope. He expects that Allah will return both children to him, indeed all three, since the third has also settled in Egypt and refuses to leave. In the broken heart of this aged father there is still a remarkable hope. This is prophetic insight!

Verse 83

Your souls have made a great matter seem easy to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all back to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. [Quranic quotations are rendered in plain meaning within ﴿ ﴾ markers only where the original quotes the verse.]

Note: the passage given to me begins with the commentary on this verse, so I have translated that commentary as follows.

Your souls have made a great sin seem easy to you. You plot against your brothers. I can only bear patience. These were the words that Hazrat Yaqoob (peace be upon him) said at the time of Yusuf's (peace be upon him) disappearance too. But on this occasion he also expresses a hope that perhaps Allah will return them all to him. Indeed Allah alone is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. He knows my circumstances too, and He knows the reality of the statements of the sons. He knows the reality of the events and trials too, and whenever the wisdom of Allah requires it, all events and facts will come to light.

From where did this ray of hope come into the heart of this old man? It was a ray of hope in Allah, he had a deep connection with the Divine Being. He had firm certainty in Allah and His mercy. And this certainty is clearly seen in the hearts of Allah's chosen servants. And for them this certainty is so sensitive that, in comparison to it, the perception of the five senses appears diminished.

This is a deeply affecting portrait of a grieving father. He feels that he is alone in bearing this sorrow; the hearts of his family do not share in it. They are not in harmony with him, nor do they stand in solidarity with him. Therefore he has withdrawn and sat alone, apart from them.

Before this, he had suffered a blow in the loss of Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he could not forget it. Even after a long time had passed, the wound of that loss had not diminished. Now a fresh blow has come in the form of the arrest of Yusuf's younger brother, and because of it the old wounds have also been reopened. His patience, which is beautiful (sabr jamil), is now close to overflowing.

Yusufali's rendering of (12:84): "Ah, my grief for Yusuf!" A person hides his sorrows and bears them; his limbs break down, his eyes turn white from grief, and this sorrow keeps consuming him from within.

"And his eyes turned white with grief, and he was suppressing his anguish within" (12:84).

But the hearts of his other sons were so filled with envy of Yusuf (peace be upon him) that they did not even feel pity for their aged father's condition. Such was their hardness of heart that even this boundless love of their father had no effect upon them. Instead of offering condolence, or kindling the lamp of hope in his heart, they increased his despair and sought to extinguish even the last ray of hope.

This is an extremely wicked and bitter statement, poisoned by envy and malice. By God, you are destroying yourself in remembrance of Yusuf (peace be upon him). Do you not see that you have been reduced to wasting away? What benefit is there now in this grief, this lamentation? Everything has a limit. Yusuf (peace be upon him) is gone, and he is not going to return.

But Yaqub (peace be upon him) rejects their words. He says: "Leave me alone. My grief and my complaint are to Allah alone. My relationship is with my Lord, and I know from Allah what you do not know."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 12, verse 86:

Verse No. 86

These words show how deep the awareness of the sovereignty and absolute authority of Allah is in the heart of a Prophet. Those who have reached Allah also feel His bounties, and they have a profound awareness of the majesty of Allah.

As for the apparent circumstances concerning Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him), they were extremely disheartening, and a long time had already passed. Hope of his being alive had been cut off altogether, let alone the hope that he would invite his father to come to him. As a result of this disheartening situation, his sons expressed strong resentment at his fresh inquiry. But none of these circumstances could affect the firm hope that this servant of Allah held in Allah. This is because his connection with his Lord was deep, and he knew about his Lord what other people did not know, since those realities were hidden from their eyes, especially concerning this event.

This is the worth of true faith and the glory of true recognition of Allah. When the servants of Allah attain recognition, they receive manifestations, they live in the world of witnessing, they are bound to the power and decree of Allah, and the watchfulness and mercy of Allah are with them. They know how Allah treats His righteous servants.

These words, "wa a'lamu min Allahi ma la ta'lamun" (12:86), meaning "and I know from Allah what you do not know," are such that this reality is so evident in them that we cannot express it in our own sentences in any way. Only the person who has been given a special taste for patience, like Hadrat Ya'qub (peace be upon him), can understand this; only such people can know what the meaning of these words is.

And for those hearts in which this kind of taste has arisen, that is, the taste for recognition of Allah, even if a rain of difficulties and hardships pours down upon them, it has no effect on them, except that the connection of such hearts with Allah, their taste for recognition and their witnessing of the Truth become even stronger.

I have no power to say anything beyond this, but I give thanks to Allah that His favour upon me is very great. The nature of my relationship with Him is known to Him or to me. He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

Now Hadrat Ya'qub (peace be upon him) turns to the search for Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brothers, and tells the sons not to despair: Allah's mercy is very vast, and there is a possibility that they will all be found together. The door of the mercy of Allah remains open at all times.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 87:

Verse 87

This is the voice of a heart that is connected to Allah!! "My sons, go and search for Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah." Use all your senses: search with great tenderness, with keen eyes, and with steadfastness. Never show despair at the grace and bounty of Allah. Here the word (rooh, spirit) is used for the mercy of Allah. It points deeply to the mercy of Allah, and it also contains the indication that after hardships, a period of ease is about to come, because after life-consuming difficulties the soul is about to receive refreshment from the dew of Allah's mercy.

﴿وَلَا تَيْأَسُوا مِن رَّوْحِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُ لَا يَيْأَسُ مِن رَّوْحِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾ (12:87) "Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people." Those believers whose hearts are connected to Allah, upon whose souls falls the dew of recognition of Allah, and over whom blow the refreshing, pleasant breezes of the mercy of Allah, never despair of the grace and bounty of Allah, even when hardships become unbearable and their hearts rise up to their throats. The believer is always under the shade of faith; he is bound to Allah through his connection with Allah. He has trust in his Lord, and this trust remains alive even in the greatest anguish and pain.

Now for the third time the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) enter the city of Egypt. The famine has left them in a wretched state. Their cash is finished; they have brought along poor-quality goods and money, and they have nothing else left. They enter in a condition where their spirit is broken, and they are no longer in a position to speak of past matters. The complaint they made about their destitution on this occasion makes their condition clear.

Verse 88

When Yusuf (peace be upon him) saw that his brothers had become so worn down, that such humility had come upon them, and that they were making appeals for mercy, he could no longer continue displaying his rank and station. It was no longer possible for him to keep his identity hidden from them. The lesson he had intended to teach them had been taught. Now the time had come to give them the great surprise for which they were wholly unprepared. They had no idea that they were standing in the court of Yusuf (peace be upon him). Accordingly, he graciously reveals his true identity to them. He makes them aware: "Do you remember what you did in the past?" This was a secret of his life, and he had told no one about it; only Allah knew.

Verse 89

Now a voice reached their ears which seemed familiar to them. The features of Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) now appeared to them as the face of someone they had seen before. Until then they had found themselves before the Aziz of Egypt, apparently, and could not even imagine that this person might be Yusuf (peace be upon him), because they were under the awe of the royal court. But now, from a distance, it became clear to them that this is the face of a brother.

Verse No. 90

Now they became certain and said: "Are you indeed Yusuf (peace be upon him)?" He said: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother." (Note: the Urdu passage gives the verse's sense as "Now they were convinced and said that you are indeed Yusuf (peace be upon him). Hadrat Yusuf (peace be upon him) suddenly revealed himself, and in summary he told them what they had done to their brother Yusuf (peace be upon him) out of ignorance. He mentions nothing more than this, and recounts the blessings of Allah that came upon him and his brother. These blessings came because we did not let the hem of taqwa (God-consciousness) and sabr (patience) slip from our hands, and all this is the result of Allah's system of justice. He gives good reward to the muttaqin (God-conscious) and the sabirin (patient).

But what was the effect of this sudden disclosure upon those brothers? Before their eyes, the entire shameful situation that they had been creating with Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother took concrete form. They are extremely ashamed. The one they had wronged stands before them as a benefactor; the one they had treated with hardheartedness is extremely forbearing; and the one they had oppressed is generous and a doer of good. Now, what else could they say?

Verse 91

They openly acknowledged their error and confessed their sin. They realised that Allah had preferred Yusuf over them, because he was forbearing, God-fearing and a doer of good. In response to their frank admission, Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) forgives them wholeheartedly. In this way their sense of shame is lessened, and forgiveness and overlooking faults is indeed the custom of the generous. Just as Yusuf (peace be upon him) succeeded in hardships, so too he succeeds in the trial of power. Surely he was among the doers of good.

Verse 92

Today there is no reproach upon you, and no retribution; and you need not feel any shame. I have removed all rancour from my heart. May Allah also forgive you; He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. Now the discourse turns to another important matter: the concern of that father whose eyes have turned white in waiting for Yusuf (peace be upon him) now weighs upon the heart. First of all, it is necessary to give him the good news; first of all, it is an obligation to meet him; it is necessary to remove the rancour from their hearts; and it is necessary to free him as quickly as possible from the physical and spiritual distress he is in; and above all, his eyesight!

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verse 93:

Verse 93

The question is: how did Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) know that his father's lost eyesight would be restored by the smell of his shirt? This is the knowledge that Allah had given him. At times, in sudden joy and sudden grief, such miracles do occur, and Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) is a Nabi and a Rasul, and Prophet Yaqub (peace be upon him) is also a Nabi and a Rasul.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 12, verses 94–95:

Now, on the other side, the scene in Canaan also brings unexpected revelations, and the scenes of Canaan end with the final fulfilment of the dream that Yusuf (peace be upon him) saw in his childhood.

Verses 94 to 95

The scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him)! What is this that they are saying? Can anyone imagine that after such a long period Yusuf (peace be upon him) is still alive, and that this old man is smelling his fragrance! ... That is why he says: "I perceive the scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him), if you do not think me senile. In truth, I am perceiving this fragrance."

The question is this: the caravan set out from Egypt, and at the same time in Canaan he perceives the scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him). How did this happen? Did he begin to smell it when the caravan left Egypt? Some commentators say that the caravan departed from Egypt and he caught the scent from that distance. But the verse does not explicitly mention Egypt. It is possible that when the caravan separated at a junction near Canaan, the fragrance reached him at the place where Yaqub (peace be upon him) was residing.

This does not mean that we consider perceiving this scent from the distance of Egypt as a miracle, which is impossible. It is possible that it was a miracle, because both Yusuf (peace be upon him) and Yaqub (peace be upon him) are prophets. Our aim and method is that we should pause at what the verse of the Qur'an conveys, especially when no narration with a authentic chain has been transmitted supporting an additional meaning for the verse. Here too, there is no authentic narration transmitted that this fragrance came from Egypt. One should not derive such a meaning merely from conjecture or implication (dalalat al-nass).

However, those who were sitting around Yaqub (peace be upon him) did not have that perception which the Lord had granted to him. Therefore, they did not perceive the scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him).

Qalu ta-Allahi innaka lafi dalalika al-qadim (12:95): "They said, 'By Allah, you are surely in your old error.'" You are still caught in your old misconception, still awaiting Yusuf (peace be upon him), although he has set out on paths from which there is no return. Yet throughout this whole story there are miracles and intimate supplications at every turn.
